To enable caching in browsers
To indicate the response is binary data
To compress the response body
questions.explanation: Including charset=utf-8 removes guessing by browsers, avoiding garbled characters especially in old browsers.

questions.question: If a handler calls res.json(undefined), what will be sent in the response body?
options: An empty string
null
undefined
An error is thrown
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify(undefined) returns undefined, so the framework treats it as null to send a valid response.

questions.question: What does res.send do when given a Buffer and no content-type header is set?
options: Sets content-type to application/octet-stream and sends the buffer
Throws an error because content-type is missing
Sends the buffer as JSON
Converts the buffer to a string and sends as HTML
questions.explanation: res.send detects a Buffer, sets content-type to application/octet-stream if none set, and calls end with the buffer.

questions.question: Why is converting binary data to a string and back a classic bug when sending responses?
options: Because bytes outside valid UTF-8 get mangled during string conversion
Because strings cannot be sent over sockets
Because string conversion increases response size
Because it causes a memory leak
questions.explanation: Converting binary to string and back mangles bytes outside valid UTF-8, corrupting binary data like images.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to send large binary files to avoid excessive memory use?
options: Convert the file to a base64 string and send as JSON
Split the file into small strings and send sequentially
Use streams with fs.createReadStream and pipe into the socket
Read the entire file into a Buffer and send at once
questions.explanation: Streaming with fs.createReadStream avoids loading large files fully into memory, preventing high RAM usage.

questions.question: What does res.status(201).json({}) do in the response object?
options: Sends a plain text response with status 201
Sets the status code to 201 and sends a JSON response
Sends an HTML response with status 201
Sets a header named 'json' to 201
questions.explanation: res.status sets the status code and res.json stringifies the object and sends it with the application/json content-type.

questions.question: Why are header names lowercased in both the request and response objects?
options: To make headers case-sensitive
To improve performance by shortening header names
To avoid duplicates like Content-Type and content-type causing bugs
Because HTTP requires lowercase headers
questions.explanation: Lowercasing header names avoids duplicates and bugs caused by case-insensitive headers being treated differently.

questions.question: What happens if res.end is called twice on the same response object?
options: The connection is reset automatically
The second call is ignored silently
An error is thrown because headers were already sent
The second call overwrites the first response
questions.explanation: If headersSent is true, res.end throws an error to loudly detect the bug of writing twice.

questions.question: How does res.redirect(url, status) work internally?
options: Sets the location header, sets the status code, and calls end with an empty body
Only sets the status code and does not send a body
Sends a JSON response with the redirect URL
Sets a custom header and leaves the status as 200
questions.explanation: res.redirect sets the location header, status code (default 302), and calls end with an empty body.

questions.question: Why does the response object add a Date header automatically?
options: To track when the response was sent for debugging
To synchronize with client clocks
To indicate the time the server started
Because HTTP servers should send a Date header as per the HTTP spec
questions.explanation: HTTP spec says servers should send a Date header, so the response adds it as a default.

questions.question: What is the advantage of the fluent interface design in the res object?
options: Prevents any mutation of the response
Automatically converts all responses to JSON
Disables setting headers after the response is sent
Allows chaining methods like res.status(404).send('Not found') for readable code
questions.explanation: Returning this from methods enables chaining, making code read like a sentence.

questions.question: What does app.decorate do in the plugin system?
options: Registers a route prefix for a group of routes
Adds a property to the app and throws an error if the name already exists
Creates a child app object with inherited properties
Adds middleware to the request pipeline
questions.explanation: app.decorate sets app at the given name to a value and throws an error if that name already exists, preventing silent overwrites.

questions.question: How does app.decorate help prevent plugin conflicts?
options: It merges decorations silently to avoid errors
It throws an error if a decoration name is already used
It automatically prefixes all decorations with plugin names
It disables decorations if duplicates are detected
questions.explanation: app.decorate throws an error if the decoration name already exists, preventing silent overwrites that cause plugin conflicts.

questions.question: If a plugin wants to add a database client only visible to its own routes, how should it use app.decorate?
options: Register the plugin without any prefix
Use app.use middleware instead of decorate
Call decorate on the child app object inside a prefix to scope it
Call decorate on the root app to make it global
questions.explanation: Decorations on a child app created with a prefix are scoped to that plugin only and not visible globally.

questions.question: What happens if two plugins try to decorate the app with the same name?
options: Both decorations are merged into an array
The second plugin silently overwrites the first decoration
The app crashes without error handling
The second call throws an error to prevent overwriting
questions.explanation: app.decorate throws an error if the name already exists, avoiding silent overwrites between plugins.

questions.question: Why does app.decorate throw an error on duplicate names instead of silently overwriting?
options: To improve performance by avoiding checks
To automatically rename conflicting decorations
To allow plugins to share the same decoration safely
To fail early and provide a clear message about plugin conflicts
questions.explanation: Throwing an error on duplicates helps detect conflicts early and prevents plugins from breaking each other silently.

The function executes slower because it is interpreted
The function is scanned twice: once during preparsing and once during full parsing
questions.explanation: Lazy parsing causes double scanning of a function when called, which is extra work but improves startup time overall.

questions.question: Why must the preparser track outer variables referenced by inner functions during lazy parsing?
options: Because it executes the inner functions during preparsing
Because it generates bytecode for those variables immediately
Because those variables may need to be stored in a heap context for closures
Because it ignores outer variables completely
questions.explanation: Tracking outer variables is necessary to decide if they must live in heap contexts accessible by closures.

questions.question: What is the scanner's job in V8?
options: To execute JavaScript code
To take raw text and split it into the smallest meaningful pieces called tokens
To generate bytecode from the AST
To build the abstract syntax tree from tokens
questions.explanation: The scanner reads raw text and produces tokens, which are the smallest meaningful pieces for parsing.

questions.question: Which of the following does the scanner skip when tokenizing?
options: Whitespace and comments
Operators and punctuation
Identifiers and numbers
Keywords like function and return
questions.explanation: Whitespace and comments are skipped by the scanner because they are not meaningful to the machine.

questions.question: How does the scanner distinguish the keyword `return` from an identifier named `returnValue`?
options: By the presence of whitespace after the word
By looking up identifiers in a keyword table
By checking the length of the word
By the position in the code
questions.explanation: The scanner uses a keyword table to recognize keywords and differentiate them from similar identifiers.

questions.question: Why does the scanner and parser cooperate when handling the slash character `/`?
options: Because `/` is always a division operator
Because `/` can mean division or start of a regular expression depending on context
Because `/` is ignored by the scanner
Because `/` starts a comment
questions.explanation: The slash character can represent division or a regular expression literal, so scanner and parser coordinate to interpret it correctly.

questions.question: What is a subtle cost of scanning very long JavaScript files?
options: Increased memory usage from storing all tokens permanently
More syntax errors
Slower execution of bytecode
Longer scanning time because the scanner processes all characters linearly
questions.explanation: Scanning time increases with file length because the scanner must process all characters, even if scanning is optimized.

questions.question: Why does the scanner produce tokens on demand rather than all at once?
options: To avoid syntax errors
To speed up scanning by storing tokens permanently
To execute code immediately after scanning
To keep memory usage low and allow parsing to start before the entire script is downloaded
questions.explanation: Producing tokens on demand keeps memory low and enables parsing to proceed incrementally.

questions.question: What does scope analysis determine during parsing?
options: The exact bytecode instructions for a function
The whitespace formatting of the source code
Where each variable lives: parameter, local, or outer function variable
The token types produced by the scanner
questions.explanation: Scope analysis decides the location of variables, affecting how they are stored and accessed later.

questions.question: Why is scope analysis important for closures?
options: It determines which variables must be stored in heap-allocated contexts accessible by inner functions
It converts variables to tokens
It removes unused variables from the code
It formats the source code for readability
questions.explanation: Scope analysis identifies variables captured by closures so they can be stored in heap contexts.

questions.question: If a variable is determined by scope analysis to be a parameter, where is it likely stored?
options: In a register
As a token in the scanner
In a heap-allocated context
In the abstract syntax tree
questions.explanation: Parameters can often be stored in registers for fast access as determined by scope analysis.

questions.question: How does scope analysis affect bytecode generation?
options: It creates tokens for the scanner
It influences whether variables are accessed via registers or context slots in the bytecode
It removes semicolons from the source code
It determines the order of bytecode instructions
questions.explanation: Scope analysis results affect how variables are accessed in bytecode, either via registers or context slots.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall if scope analysis fails to correctly identify outer variables used by inner functions?
options: Variables may be incorrectly stored in registers instead of heap contexts, breaking closures
The AST will include semicolons unnecessarily
Lazy parsing will skip the function entirely
The scanner will produce incorrect tokens
questions.explanation: Incorrect scope analysis can cause variables to be stored improperly, breaking closure behavior.

questions.question: Why must the preparser track outer variables referenced by skipped inner functions during lazy parsing?
options: To ignore outer variables completely
To generate bytecode for inner functions immediately
To execute inner functions during preparsing
To ensure those variables are stored in heap contexts if needed for closures
questions.explanation: Tracking outer variables ensures correct storage for closures even when inner functions are skipped during preparsing.

questions.question: What is tokenization in the context of V8?
options: The execution of JavaScript code
The creation of the abstract syntax tree
The generation of bytecode
The process of splitting raw source code into tokens by the scanner
questions.explanation: Tokenization is the scanner's process of splitting raw text into meaningful tokens.

questions.question: Which of the following is a token type produced by the scanner?
options: Comment
Identifier
Semicolon as a separate node
Whitespace
questions.explanation: Identifiers are tokens; whitespace and comments are skipped, and semicolons are not kept in the AST.

questions.question: If the scanner encounters the line `returnValue`, how does it tokenize it?
options: As invalid syntax
As a keyword token `return` only
As a single identifier token, not the keyword `return`
As two tokens: keyword `return` and identifier `Value`
questions.explanation: The scanner recognizes `returnValue` as an identifier, not the keyword `return`, by looking up the whole word.

questions.question: How does the scanner handle template literals with embedded expressions?
options: It switches modes to scan string parts, pauses for expressions, then resumes scanning
It ignores embedded expressions
It fails with a syntax error
It treats the entire template literal as a single token
questions.explanation: The scanner switches modes to handle template literals, scanning strings, pausing for expressions, then resuming.

questions.question: What is a subtle consequence of the scanner recording line breaks for the parser?
options: It slows down scanning significantly
It enables automatic semicolon insertion rules that affect code meaning
It prevents syntax errors
It causes the scanner to produce more tokens
questions.explanation: Line breaks recorded by the scanner allow the parser to apply automatic semicolon insertion, affecting code behavior.

questions.question: Why do minifiers reduce whitespace and shorten names with respect to tokenization?
options: To increase the number of syntax errors
To reduce the amount of work the scanner must do during tokenization
To make the AST larger
To produce more tokens for the parser
questions.explanation: Minifiers reduce whitespace and shorten names to reduce scanning work and download size.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the accumulator in V8's bytecode interpreter?
options: It holds the machine code generated by the optimizer.
It acts as a special working register for many instructions.
It manages memory allocation for local variables.
It stores all function arguments.
questions.explanation: The accumulator is a special working register used implicitly by most instructions, as explained in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: Why does V8 use an accumulator in addition to virtual registers?
options: To hold the feedback vector slots.
To reduce instruction size by having fewer explicit operands.
To store all local variables in one place.
To speed up machine code compilation.
questions.explanation: Using an accumulator reduces the number of explicit operands per instruction, making bytecode smaller and more compact, as stated in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: Given the bytecode sequence: Ldar a1, Add a0, [0], Return, which value ends up being returned by the function?
options: The sum of the values in registers a0 and a1.
The value in register a1.
The value in the feedback vector slot 0.
The value in register a0.
questions.explanation: Ldar loads a1 into the accumulator, Add adds a0 to the accumulator, and Return returns the accumulator, yielding the sum of a0 and a1 as explained in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: If a function has many local variables but reuses a single variable in the source code, what is the likely effect on the register count in the bytecode header?
options: The register count increases to track reuse.
The register count depends only on parameters, not locals.
The register count decreases due to reuse.
The register count remains the same.
questions.explanation: Reusing variables reduces the number of virtual registers needed, lowering the register count as shown in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: What is a potential downside of using an accumulator-based register machine for bytecode execution?
options: The interpreter is slower than direct machine code execution.
It prevents the use of type feedback.
It complicates the bytecode format with nested expressions.
It requires more memory than machine code.
questions.explanation: Interpretation of bytecode with an accumulator is slower than running direct machine code, as noted in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: Why does the add instruction in V8 bytecode take one operand from a register and the other implicitly from the accumulator?
options: Because the accumulator cannot hold two values simultaneously.
To allow the optimizer to ignore the accumulator.
To minimize instruction size by having fewer explicit operands.
Because registers cannot be used as output operands.
questions.explanation: This design reduces instruction operand count, making bytecode smaller and more compact, as explained in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: What is Ignition in the context of V8?
options: The interpreter that runs V8 bytecode.
The optimizing compiler that generates machine code.
The garbage collector for JavaScript objects.
The virtual machine that executes machine code.
questions.explanation: Ignition is the bytecode interpreter that runs the V8 bytecode, as introduced in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: Why did V8 switch from compiling directly to machine code to using bytecode and Ignition?
options: To eliminate the need for an optimizing compiler.
To increase the speed of machine code generation.
To reduce memory usage and improve startup time.
To allow JavaScript to run on the GPU.
questions.explanation: Bytecode is more compact and cheaper to generate, reducing memory and startup costs, as explained in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: If a function is never called, what happens to its bytecode in V8?
options: It is never generated due to lazy compilation.
It is optimized immediately.
It is stored as machine code.
It is generated but never executed.
questions.explanation: Lazy compilation means uncalled functions do not have bytecode generated, as noted in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: How does Ignition use type feedback collected during bytecode interpretation?
options: It stores feedback only for debugging purposes.
It skips interpretation and runs machine code directly.
It modifies the bytecode to add more instructions.
It provides input to the optimizing compiler for better machine code.
questions.explanation: Type feedback collected during interpretation is used by the optimizing compiler to generate efficient machine code, as explained in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: What is a trade-off of using Ignition's bytecode interpreter compared to running optimized machine code?
options: Interpretation requires multiple CPU cores.
Interpretation cannot handle loops.
Interpretation is slower but uses less memory and starts faster.
Interpretation is faster but uses more memory.
questions.explanation: Interpretation is slower but reduces memory use and improves startup time, a trade-off discussed in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: What is a key trade-off involved in using Ignition's bytecode interpreter instead of compiling directly to optimized machine code?
options: The interpreter requires more memory because bytecode is bulkier than machine code.
The interpreter cannot collect type feedback, limiting optimization opportunities.
The interpreter is slower because each bytecode instruction must be fetched, decoded, and dispatched, despite being more memory efficient.
The interpreter is only compatible with Intel processors, reducing portability.
questions.explanation: Ignition's bytecode interpreter is slower than optimized machine code because every instruction must be fetched, decoded, and dispatched, though it saves memory and improves startup time.

questions.question: Why does V8 use a single byte for each opcode in its bytecode format?
options: To simplify the optimizing compiler.
Because JavaScript only has 256 operations.
To keep instructions small and the bytecode compact.
To match the size of machine code instructions.
questions.explanation: Each opcode fits in one byte to keep the bytecode small and compact, as stated in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: What information is included in the bytecode header printed by V8?
options: Opcode names and operand counts.
Machine code addresses and sizes.
Parameter count, register count, and frame size.
Source code line numbers.
questions.explanation: The header includes parameter count, register count, and frame size, as described in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: If a function has two parameters and a receiver, what will the parameter count in the bytecode header be?
options: Four, including the feedback slots.
Three, because the receiver counts as one parameter.
Two, only the function parameters count.
One, the receiver only.
questions.explanation: Parameter count includes the receiver plus function parameters, totaling three as explained in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: Why does the add instruction sometimes load the second operand before the first in V8 bytecode?
options: Because the add instruction uses the accumulator and one register operand, requiring a specific load order.
Because feedback slots require operands to be reversed.
Because the accumulator can only hold the first operand.
Because the bytecode generator randomly orders operands.
questions.explanation: The add instruction takes one operand from a register and one from the accumulator, so the generator chooses an order fitting this pattern, as explained in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of having a uniform bytecode format in V8?
options: It serves as a single representation for interpretation, optimization, and deoptimization.
It allows skipping the interpreter entirely.
It eliminates the need for virtual registers.
It enables direct execution on all hardware without translation.
questions.explanation: A uniform bytecode format is used for interpretation, optimization input, and deoptimization targets, simplifying the engine as stated in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: How does V8's bytecode format contribute to the engine's portability?
options: Bytecode is compiled directly to platform-specific machine code.
Portability is achieved by avoiding bytecode altogether.
Each platform uses a different bytecode format.
The same bytecode is generated on all platforms; only execution and machine code generation differ.
questions.explanation: The bytecode generation is uniform across platforms, with only execution and machine code generation varying, as explained in Lecture 3.1.

questions.question: What are virtual registers in V8 bytecode execution?
options: Slots in the function's stack frame holding locals and temporaries.
Memory locations storing machine code.
Physical CPU registers used by the interpreter.
Feedback vector slots for type information.
questions.explanation: Virtual registers are stack frame slots holding local variables and temporaries, not actual CPU registers, as described in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: What naming convention does V8 use for function arguments in virtual registers?
options: Arguments are named a0, a1, a2, etc.
Arguments use the names of the source variables.
Arguments are stored in the accumulator.
Arguments are named r0, r1, r2, etc.
questions.explanation: Function arguments live in registers named a0, a1, etc., as explained in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: If a function has one local variable and two parameters, how many virtual registers might the bytecode header report?
options: Two registers for parameters only.
Zero registers because parameters don't count.
Three registers for parameters and local combined.
One register for the local variable; parameters are separate.
questions.explanation: The register count reflects local variables and temporaries, so one register for the local variable is typical as explained in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: How does reusing a single virtual register for multiple variables affect the bytecode?
options: It prevents the use of the accumulator.
It increases the number of instructions required.
It reduces the total number of registers needed, making bytecode smaller.
It causes the interpreter to run slower.
questions.explanation: Reusing registers reduces register count and bytecode size, as shown in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: Why does the accumulator and virtual register design disappear after TurboFan optimization?
options: Because TurboFan runs the interpreter instead.
Because virtual registers become physical CPU registers.
Because TurboFan builds its own representation independent of the bytecode machine.
Because the accumulator is replaced by the feedback vector.
questions.explanation: TurboFan creates its own IR and no longer uses the accumulator or virtual registers from bytecode, as explained in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: What is a misconception about the accumulator's role in performance?
options: That it stores all function arguments.
That it runs machine code directly.
That it is primarily a performance trick rather than a size optimization.
That it eliminates the need for virtual registers.
questions.explanation: The accumulator is mainly a size optimization with some speed side effects, not primarily a performance trick, as clarified in Lecture 3.3.

questions.question: What distinguishes just-in-time (JIT) compilation from ahead-of-time compilation?
options: JIT compiles the entire program before running, while ahead-of-time compiles on the fly
JIT uses only interpreters without generating machine code
Ahead-of-time compilation optimizes only hot loops during execution
JIT compiles code while the program runs, only for hot code, whereas ahead-of-time compiles the whole program before running
questions.explanation: JIT compiles code on the fly during execution for code that is hot, unlike ahead-of-time which compiles the whole program before running.

questions.question: Why does V8 use thresholds before optimizing functions with TurboFan?
options: To prevent any function from running in the interpreter
To ensure all functions are compiled immediately for maximum speed
Because TurboFan cannot compile functions called less than ten times
To avoid spending compile time on code that is unlikely to be reused and to balance startup speed
questions.explanation: Thresholds prevent wasting compile time on code that won't repay it and avoid slowing startup by compiling everything immediately.

questions.question: If a function is called only once but contains a very hot loop, how does V8 optimize it?
options: By interpreting the loop without any optimization
By using on-stack replacement to swap the running frame to optimized code during the loop
By compiling the whole function ahead-of-time before running the loop
By ignoring optimization since the function was called only once
questions.explanation: V8 uses on-stack replacement to optimize hot loops even if the surrounding function runs only once.

questions.question: In a scenario where a function is called many times with stable input types, what does V8 do to improve performance?
options: Keeps interpreting the function without optimization
Disables the function to avoid overhead
Compiles the function ahead-of-time before any calls happen
Marks the function as hot and compiles it with TurboFan to optimized machine code
questions.explanation: When a function is hot and stable, V8 marks it for optimization and compiles it with TurboFan for better performance.

questions.question: What is the main reason V8 does not optimize every function immediately?
options: Because TurboFan cannot compile functions with loops
To avoid slowing startup and wasting compile time on code that is not hot or stable
Because the interpreter does not collect any feedback
Because all functions are optimized immediately
questions.explanation: V8 waits for functions to be hot and stable to ensure optimization effort is worthwhile and startup remains fast.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of relying heavily on JIT optimization in V8?
options: Functions with inconsistent or rare input types can cause frequent deoptimizations, leading to performance cliffs
JIT compilers never use CPU resources
Optimized code always uses more memory but never fails
All functions are always optimized perfectly with no downsides
questions.explanation: Inconsistent input types cause repeated deoptimizations, which degrade performance and cause the 'performance cliff'.

questions.question: What role does type feedback play in TurboFan's optimization?
options: It disables guards to speed up code
It records the types seen at operations to guide speculation and generate fast specialized code
It forces TurboFan to generate generic code that handles all types equally
It prevents TurboFan from optimizing any code with dynamic types
questions.explanation: Type feedback records operand types seen to let TurboFan speculate and generate fast code specialized for those types.

questions.question: Why does mixing types for a variable reduce the benefits of speculation?
options: Because TurboFan crashes when types are mixed
Because the feedback becomes more general, forcing TurboFan to generate slower, more generic code
Because guards are removed when types differ
Because the interpreter stops collecting feedback
questions.explanation: Mixed types cause feedback slots to generalize, so TurboFan generates more general and slower code.

questions.question: If a function is optimized very early with limited input types, what risk does this pose?
options: It makes the function run slower than interpreted code
It may cause deoptimization later when encountering broader real-world input types
It guarantees the function will never deoptimize
It disables guards in the optimized code
questions.explanation: Early optimization with narrow input types can cause deoptimization when later inputs differ from the initial feedback.

questions.question: How does TurboFan use guards in its generated code?
options: Guards prevent any type checking to maximize speed
Guards check assumptions at runtime and trigger deoptimization if violated, ensuring safety of speculation
Guards compile code ahead-of-time
Guards always cause the code to run slower than interpreted code
questions.explanation: Guards verify the assumptions made by speculation and cause deoptimization if those assumptions fail.

questions.question: What is a key trade-off involved in TurboFan's speculation based on type feedback?
options: Always slower code but guaranteed correctness without deoptimization
No need for guards but increased memory usage
Faster code for expected types but risk of deoptimization if unexpected types appear
Speculation disables all optimizations to avoid errors
questions.explanation: Speculation bets on expected types for speed but requires deoptimization if inputs violate assumptions.

questions.question: Why might repeated optimize-deoptimize cycles occur for a function in V8?
options: Because V8 only optimizes functions once and never deoptimizes
Because the interpreter disables optimization after the first call
Because TurboFan cannot generate machine code for loops
Because the function sees varying input types that invalidate previous assumptions, causing V8 to repeatedly reoptimize
questions.explanation: Changing input types cause assumptions to fail repeatedly, leading to cycles of optimization and deoptimization.

questions.question: What does V8 call the hidden description of an object's layout?
options: Map
Dictionary
Hidden class
Shape
questions.explanation: Inside V8, the hidden description of an object's layout is called a Map, which is different from the JavaScript Map collection.

questions.question: Why does V8 use hidden classes for objects?
options: To keep property names in alphabetical order
To store all properties in a hash table
To replace expensive dictionary lookups with cheap shape checks
To allow properties to be added or removed at any time
questions.explanation: Hidden classes replace expensive dictionary lookups with cheap shape checks, enabling fast property access.

questions.question: If two objects are created by the same constructor and property assignments in the same order, what can be said about their hidden classes?
options: Their hidden classes depend on property values
They share the same hidden class
They have no hidden class
They have different hidden classes
questions.explanation: Objects created the same way, with the same property order, share one hidden class.

questions.question: What happens to the hidden class when properties are added in a different order?
options: A new hidden class is created for the different order
The hidden class merges both orders
The object loses its hidden class
The hidden class remains the same
questions.explanation: Different property addition orders lead to different hidden classes because they follow different paths in the shape transition tree.

questions.question: Why is it important to initialize properties in the same order in JavaScript objects?
options: To enable garbage collection
To avoid dictionary mode and keep shape sharing
To allow properties to be deleted safely
To reduce memory usage
questions.explanation: Initializing properties in the same order keeps shape sharing intact and avoids dictionary mode, which slows down property access.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of using `delete` on object properties in V8?
options: It speeds up property access
It forces the object into dictionary mode, losing shape sharing
It creates a new hidden class with the same properties
It causes the hidden class to merge with others
questions.explanation: Using `delete` often forces V8 to switch the object into dictionary mode, which disables shape sharing and slows down access.

questions.question: What does an inline cache (IC) store for a property access site on its first execution?
options: The property name and value
The full object layout
The dictionary of all properties
The hidden class and property offset
questions.explanation: On first execution, the IC stores the pair of the object's hidden class and the offset of the property for quick future access.

questions.question: What state is an inline cache in when it has seen exactly one hidden class at a property access site?
options: Monomorphic
Uninitialized
Megamorphic
Polymorphic
questions.explanation: When an IC has seen exactly one shape, it is in the monomorphic state, which is the fastest.

questions.question: If a function accesses a property on objects from two different hidden classes, what is the inline cache state?
options: Polymorphic
Uninitialized
Monomorphic
Megamorphic
questions.explanation: Seeing two shapes at a site makes the IC polymorphic, storing multiple shape-offset pairs.

questions.question: What happens to the inline cache when a property access site encounters many different hidden classes?
options: It becomes polymorphic
It becomes megamorphic and stops caching per site
It resets to uninitialized
It stays monomorphic
questions.explanation: When too many shapes are seen, the IC becomes megamorphic and falls back to a slower global lookup.

questions.question: Why does a megamorphic inline cache slow down optimized code?
options: Because it caches too many shapes
Because it removes hidden classes
Because it stops caching per site and uses a generic runtime call
Because it merges all shapes into one
questions.explanation: Megamorphic ICs stop caching per site and use a generic runtime call, preventing further optimization.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall that causes megamorphic inline caches?
options: Using too many object literals
Creating objects with the same property order
Deleting properties from objects
Using a helper function that accesses properties on many unrelated object types
questions.explanation: Helpers called with many unrelated object types accumulate many shapes in one IC, causing megamorphic state.

questions.question: What is the initial shape of a new JavaScript object in V8?
options: Dictionary shape
Shape with default properties
Empty shape with no properties
Shape with all possible properties
questions.explanation: A new object starts with an empty shape that has no properties.

questions.question: What is a shape transition in V8?
options: Moving an object to a new shape that includes a newly added property
Merging two shapes into one
Mutating an existing shape to add a property
Deleting a property from a shape
questions.explanation: A shape transition moves the object to a new shape that includes the added property, without mutating the old shape.

questions.question: If two objects have the same properties but added in different orders, what can be said about their shapes?
options: They have different shapes
They share the same hidden class but different shapes
They have no shape
They share the same shape
questions.explanation: Different property addition orders lead to different shape transitions and thus different shapes.

questions.question: Why does V8 build a tree of shapes?
options: To track all possible property names alphabetically
To record sequences of property additions and enable shape sharing
To optimize garbage collection
To store property values efficiently
questions.explanation: The tree structure records sequences of property additions as shape transitions, enabling shape sharing among objects.

questions.question: What is the consequence of creating objects with different property addition orders on inline cache performance?
options: It improves inline cache monomorphism
It has no effect on inline caches
It merges inline caches into a single monomorphic cache
It causes polymorphic or megamorphic inline caches, slowing down property access
questions.explanation: Different shapes from different property orders cause polymorphic or megamorphic ICs, which are slower.

questions.question: Why does V8 prefer object literals with properties in the same order across the code?
options: To create objects with the same final shape directly, avoiding shape transitions
To reduce memory usage
To enable dictionary mode
To avoid using hidden classes
questions.explanation: Object literals with consistent property order allow V8 to build the final shape immediately, skipping transition steps.

questions.question: What are the three phases of the mark-sweep-compact algorithm used in V8's major garbage collection?
options: Marking, Sweeping, Compaction
Copying, Marking, Sweeping
Scanning, Copying, Compacting
Allocation, Promotion, Deallocation
questions.explanation: The mark-sweep-compact algorithm consists of marking reachable objects, sweeping unreachable ones, and optionally compacting fragmented memory.

questions.question: In the mark-sweep-compact process, what color represents objects that have been fully processed?
options: White
Grey
Red
Black
questions.explanation: Black means an object is fully processed during the marking phase.

questions.question: If a V8 program retains many objects in the old generation causing frequent Mark-Compact collections, what is a likely consequence?
options: Faster minor collections with less copying
Reduced memory fragmentation in the young generation
Longer pause times due to heavier major collections
Immediate promotion of all young objects
questions.explanation: Retaining many objects in the old generation causes more frequent and heavier major collections, increasing pause times.

questions.question: During the sweeping phase of mark-sweep-compact, what does V8 do with unmarked objects?
options: Turns their space into free blocks without moving objects
Copies them to a new memory area
Promotes them to the young generation
Compacts them to reduce fragmentation
questions.explanation: Sweeping frees memory occupied by unmarked objects by marking their space as free, without moving live objects.

questions.question: Why does V8 perform compaction only selectively during the major GC?
options: Because compaction moves all objects regardless of fragmentation
Because compaction is expensive and done only when fragmentation is high
Because compaction increases pause times dramatically every time
Because compaction is unnecessary for small heaps
questions.explanation: Compaction is costly, so V8 performs it only on pages with high fragmentation to optimize pause times.

questions.question: What is the main engineering challenge addressed by the Orinoco project in V8's major GC?
options: Removing the write barrier from the collector
Reducing pause times by doing marking incrementally and concurrently
Eliminating the need for sweeping
Making compaction run on the main thread only
questions.explanation: Orinoco reduces pause times by performing marking incrementally and concurrently with program execution.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the scavenger in V8?
options: To quickly collect garbage in the young generation
To compact memory in the old generation
To allocate large objects
To generate machine code
questions.explanation: The scavenger is the minor collector that cleans the young generation quickly and often.

questions.question: What are the two semi-spaces in V8's new space called during a scavenge?
options: Young-space and Old-space
From-space and To-space
Heap-space and Stack-space
Active-space and Passive-space
questions.explanation: The two halves of new space are called from-space (active) and to-space (empty) during scavenging.

questions.question: If a program creates many short-lived objects inside a function, what effect does this have on scavenger collections?
options: Objects will be immediately promoted to old generation
Scavenges will be fast because most objects die young
Scavenges will not run at all
Scavenges will be slow because most objects survive
questions.explanation: Most short-lived objects die young, so scavenger collections are fast and efficient.

questions.question: What happens if an old object holds a pointer to a young object without a write barrier?
options: The scavenger will copy the old object instead
The young object might be incorrectly collected as garbage
The young object will be permanently retained
The old object will be promoted to the young generation
questions.explanation: Without a write barrier, the scavenger would miss references from old to young objects, wrongly collecting live young objects.

questions.question: Why does the scavenger copy survivors to the other semi-space instead of just marking them?
options: To avoid using a write barrier
To promote all survivors immediately to the old generation
To pack survivors tightly and improve cache behavior
To increase the size of the young generation
questions.explanation: Copying survivors packs them tightly in memory, improving cache locality and allocation speed.

questions.question: What is the 'mid-life crisis' pattern in V8's garbage collection behavior?
options: Objects surviving two scavenges get promoted and copied multiple times before dying in old generation
Objects that never get promoted to old generation
Objects that die immediately after allocation
Objects that cause write barrier failures
questions.explanation: Mid-life crisis is when objects survive two scavenges, get promoted, copied multiple times, then die in the old generation, causing costly cleanup.

questions.question: What is the main difference between the young generation and old generation in V8's heap layout?
options: Young generation is for machine code; old generation is for arrays
Young generation holds large objects; old generation holds small objects
Young generation is never collected; old generation is always collected
Young generation is small and collected frequently; old generation is larger and collected less often
questions.explanation: The young generation is small and collected frequently, while the old generation is larger and collected less often.

questions.question: How does V8 allocate new objects in the young generation?
options: By copying objects from the old generation
By bumping a pointer forward in the active semi-space
By searching for free blocks in the old generation
By compacting memory first
questions.explanation: New objects are allocated cheaply by bumping a pointer forward in the active semi-space of new space.

questions.question: What is the role of the large object space in V8's heap?
options: To store machine code generated by compilers
To hold all newly allocated objects
To keep the hidden classes for objects
To hold objects too big for regular pages, which are never copied
questions.explanation: Large object space holds very big objects like huge arrays or buffers that are never copied around.

questions.question: What happens to objects that survive multiple scavenges in V8's heap layout?
options: They are immediately freed
They remain in the young generation indefinitely
They get promoted to the old generation
They are moved to the large object space
questions.explanation: Objects surviving two scavenges are promoted to the old generation to avoid repeated copying.

questions.question: Why does V8 separate the heap into spaces like young generation, old generation, and large object space?
options: To store only machine code in the heap
Because different kinds of data have different lifetimes and collection needs
To allocate memory randomly across the heap
To avoid using a garbage collector
questions.explanation: Different spaces optimize for lifetimes and collection frequency, improving efficiency based on the generational hypothesis.

questions.question: How can increasing the size of the young generation semi-space affect garbage collection behavior?
options: It can reduce promotion rates for allocation-heavy servers
It increases the old generation size automatically
It causes more frequent major collections
It disables scavenger collections
questions.explanation: A larger young generation reduces how often objects get promoted, lowering old generation pressure.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a write barrier in V8's garbage collector?
options: To record pointers from old objects to young objects for correct minor collection
To speed up allocation in the young generation
To compact memory in the old generation
To allocate large objects
questions.explanation: Write barriers track references from old to young objects so the scavenger treats them as roots and avoids collecting live young objects.

questions.question: When does V8's write barrier add an entry to the remembered set?
options: When promoting an object to the old generation
When storing a pointer from an old object to a young object
When sweeping unreachable objects
When allocating a new object in the young generation
questions.explanation: The write barrier records locations when an old object is updated to point to a young object.

questions.question: How does the write barrier help maintain correctness during incremental marking in the major GC?
options: By promoting all young objects immediately
By speeding up sweeping phase
By disabling scavenger collections temporarily
By keeping track of object mutations to ensure live objects are not missed
questions.explanation: The write barrier tracks changes during marking to prevent missing live objects modified by the program.

questions.question: What is the trade-off involved in using a write barrier in V8?
options: Slower allocation speed in the young generation
Longer pause times during scavenges
A small cost on stores to enable efficient minor and major collections
Increased memory fragmentation
questions.explanation: The write barrier adds a small overhead on pointer stores to maintain GC correctness and efficiency.

questions.question: Why is forcing garbage collection with global.gc() generally discouraged in production V8 programs?
options: Because it disables the write barrier
Because it causes immediate promotion of all objects
Because it prevents scavenger collections
Because V8's heuristics know better when to collect and forcing can degrade performance
questions.explanation: Forcing collection overrides V8's optimized timing, often leading to worse performance.

questions.question: How does the write barrier interact with multi-threaded or concurrent marking in V8?
options: It promotes objects immediately to avoid race conditions
It disables concurrent marking
It ensures marking remains correct while the program mutates objects concurrently
It causes all marking to happen on the main thread only
questions.explanation: The write barrier tracks mutations during concurrent marking to maintain correctness without stopping the program.

questions.question: What is a common trigger for deoptimization related to function argument types?
options: Avoiding the use of the arguments object
Passing a string to a function optimized for integers
Using only small integers as arguments
Calling a function with the same number of arguments each time
questions.explanation: Deoptimization can be triggered when a function optimized for integers receives a string, causing the guard to fail.

questions.question: Which of the following can cause deoptimization due to shape changes?
options: Using only packed arrays without holes
An optimized property load encountering an object with a different hidden class
Passing consistent argument types to a function
Calling a function with the same function each time
questions.explanation: Deoptimization occurs if an optimized property load expects a particular hidden class but sees an object with another one, causing the guard to fail.

questions.question: If a function optimized for small integers suddenly receives a floating point number, what is likely to happen?
options: The function will convert the float to an integer automatically
The function will throw a runtime error
The function will continue running optimized without issues
The function will deoptimize due to number representation change
questions.explanation: A number representation change, such as receiving a floating point number instead of a small integer, triggers deoptimization because the guard fails.

questions.question: In a scenario where a function is repeatedly optimized and deoptimized in a loop, what is the recommended approach to fix it?
options: Use megamorphic call sites to handle multiple types
Identify the failing assumption and fix the caller or normalize the data
Increase the number of arguments passed to the function
Add more try-catch blocks around the function
questions.explanation: The method is to note the deopt reason, find which assumption failed, fix the caller or make data uniform, then rerun to confirm the deopt is gone.

questions.question: Why should you avoid adding properties to objects later in different places?
options: Because it makes the code harder to read
Because it causes syntax errors in V8
Because it spawns shape branches that degrade performance
Because it automatically deletes existing properties
questions.explanation: Adding properties later in different places causes shape branches, which breaks shape consistency and slows down optimized code.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of leaving some fields absent instead of initializing them with null?
options: It allows TurboFan to optimize the function better
It prevents deoptimization triggers related to type changes
It causes the object shape to depend on data, leading to polymorphic shapes
It improves performance by reducing memory usage
questions.explanation: Leaving fields off causes the object shape to depend on the data, creating polymorphic shapes and hurting performance.

questions.question: What defines monomorphic code at a call site or property access?
options: It is optimized for multiple argument types
It has seen many different types or shapes
It has only ever seen one type or shape
It calls many different functions
questions.explanation: Monomorphic means a call site or property access has only ever seen one type or shape.

questions.question: Why do classes and constructors help maintain monomorphic shapes?
options: Because they prevent any property additions after creation
Because every instance runs the same constructor body, ensuring shape consistency
Because they automatically inline all function calls
Because they force all objects to be megamorphic
questions.explanation: Classes and constructors make shape consistency automatic since every instance runs the same constructor body.

questions.question: If you have a hot function called with different argument types from different call sites, what is the likely impact?
options: The function will optimize better due to diverse inputs
The function will lose monomorphism and may deoptimize more often
The function will be inlined at all call sites
There will be no impact if the function is small
questions.explanation: Passing different argument types breaks monomorphism and can cause the function to deoptimize or adapt more frequently.

questions.question: How does creating objects with different property orders affect performance?
options: It forces TurboFan to inline all calls
It prevents deoptimization triggers
It creates multiple shapes, leading to polymorphic code and slower execution
It improves caching and speeds up property access
questions.explanation: Different property orders create different shapes, which cause polymorphic code and degrade performance.

questions.question: What is a trade-off when trying to keep code monomorphic by initializing absent fields with null?
options: You force the engine to use dictionary mode for objects
You increase memory usage but maintain shape consistency for better optimization
You reduce memory usage but risk deoptimization triggers
You make the code less readable without performance benefits
questions.explanation: Initializing absent fields with null uses more memory but keeps object shapes consistent, which is better for optimization.

questions.question: Why is it beneficial to keep hot code monomorphic rather than polymorphic or megamorphic?
options: Because megamorphic sites use less memory
Because monomorphic call sites allow function calls to be inlined, improving performance
Because polymorphic code is easier to read and maintain
Because polymorphic code always causes deoptimization
questions.explanation: The lecture explains that a call site always calling the same function (monomorphic) can be inlined, while polymorphic or megamorphic call sites cannot, which improves performance.

questions.question: Why should you avoid megamorphic call sites?
options: Because they call many different functions and cannot be inlined
Because they optimize better than monomorphic sites
Because they always cause runtime errors
Because they only handle one type or shape
questions.explanation: Megamorphic sites have seen many types or functions and cannot be inlined, hurting performance.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of types or shapes a call site can see to be considered polymorphic?
options: Only one
More than ten
Exactly eight
Up to about four
questions.explanation: Polymorphic means a call site has seen a few types or shapes, up to about four.

questions.question: In a scenario where a property access has seen five different shapes, how is it classified?
options: Uninitialized
Megamorphic
Monomorphic
Polymorphic
questions.explanation: More than about four shapes means the site is megamorphic.

questions.question: If a hot function is called with argument types that vary between integers, floats, and strings, what is the expected impact?
options: The function remains monomorphic and runs faster
The function will be inlined at all call sites
The function becomes polymorphic and may run slower due to deoptimizations
The function will throw a type error
questions.explanation: Varying argument types cause polymorphic behavior and can trigger deoptimizations, slowing down the function.

questions.question: What is a downside of megamorphic call sites in terms of optimization?
options: They always trigger garbage collection
They cause immediate program crashes
They cannot be inlined and lead to slower code
They improve performance by caching multiple types
questions.explanation: Megamorphic call sites cannot be inlined because they call many different functions, leading to slower code.

questions.question: Why might a polymorphic call site degrade performance compared to a monomorphic one?
options: Because it handles multiple types, preventing certain optimizations like inlining
Because it uses less memory
Because it avoids deoptimization triggers
Because it forces all arrays to be holey
questions.explanation: Polymorphic sites handle multiple types, which limits optimizations such as inlining and slows down execution.

questions.question: What does the V8 sampling profiler do when enabled with --prof?
options: Automatically optimizes all functions
Periodically samples what the program is doing and writes samples to a log
Disables garbage collection
Prevents deoptimization of hot functions
questions.explanation: The V8 sampling profiler periodically samples program execution and writes the data to a log for later analysis.

questions.question: How can you view the profiling report generated by running node with --prof?
options: Use the Chrome DevTools without any additional steps
Run node --trace-opt on the log file
Open the log file directly in a text editor
Run node --prof-process followed by the log file name
questions.explanation: The profiling log is processed with node --prof-process to generate a human-readable report.

questions.question: If a function shows a high number of ticks in the profiler, what should you do next?
options: Add more arguments to the function
Use trace flags to check optimization and deoptimization history and inspect inputs
Immediately rewrite the function in C++
Ignore it if the program runs correctly
questions.explanation: After identifying a slow function via profiling, you check its optimization status and inputs to understand performance issues.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the bottom up profile section in the --prof report?
options: It lists the heaviest functions and their callers to identify slow code paths
It shows garbage collection statistics only
It displays source code with annotations
It lists only C++ runtime functions
questions.explanation: The bottom up profile lists heavy functions and who called them, helping find slow code and call paths.

questions.question: What is a challenge when interpreting V8 sampling profiler output that the lecture highlights?
options: The log file is large and not meant for direct human reading
The profiler disables all optimizations
It prevents garbage collection
It only works on small scripts
questions.explanation: The profiler produces large log files that require processing to be understandable by humans.

questions.question: Why is it important to profile under realistic, warmed-up load rather than from a cold start?
options: Because cold start profiling only shows C++ functions
Because warm-up causes immediate deoptimization
Because V8 optimizations and deoptimizations settle over time, affecting performance profiles
Because cold start profiling disables the profiler
questions.explanation: V8's optimization behavior changes as the program runs longer, so realistic warmed-up profiling gives more accurate results.

questions.question: What is the main difference between polling and long-polling in terms of server response?
options: Polling holds the request until data is available, while long-polling sends requests regularly.
Polling sends a request regularly regardless of new data, while long-polling holds the request until data is available or timeout.
Polling uses WebSockets, while long-polling uses HTTP requests.
Polling is push-based, while long-polling is pull-based.
questions.explanation: Polling sends requests at intervals regardless of new data, whereas long-polling holds the request open until there is data or a timeout.

questions.question: What is a key cost of long-polling compared to polling?
options: It cannot handle timeouts.
It requires more frequent requests than polling.
Each waiting client holds an open request, increasing server connection state.
It uses WebSocket frames for communication.
questions.explanation: Long-polling keeps requests open until data is available, so each waiting client holds an open request, increasing server state.

questions.question: If a chat application uses long-polling with a 30-second timeout, what happens when a message arrives just after the server responds to a client request?
options: The message is lost because the client is not connected.
The client opens a new request immediately, so the message is delivered with minimal latency.
The client must wait until the next polling interval to receive the message.
The server sends the message on the same open request.
questions.explanation: After the server responds, the client immediately opens a new request, allowing the next message to be delivered quickly.

questions.question: How does long-polling reduce wasted requests compared to polling?
options: By using WebSocket connections.
By holding requests open until data is available, it avoids frequent empty responses.
By caching messages on the client.
By sending requests more frequently.
questions.explanation: Long-polling holds requests open until there is data, so it avoids many empty responses that polling would send.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of long-polling related to message delivery during reconnect gaps?
options: The server cannot handle multiple clients.
Events can slip by unless message IDs are tracked carefully.
It requires WebSocket support on the client.
Latency is always higher than polling.
questions.explanation: Because of reconnect gaps between long-polling requests, events can be missed unless IDs are tracked carefully.

questions.question: Why does long-polling still incur overhead per message despite holding requests open?
options: Because it multiplexes multiple messages in one request.
Because it uses WebSocket frames for every message.
Each message requires a full HTTP round trip with headers, and the client needs a second request to send data.
Because it caches messages on the server.
questions.explanation: Long-polling uses full HTTP requests and responses for each message, including headers, and sending data requires a separate request.

questions.question: In plain polling, how often does the client typically send requests to check for new data?
options: Continuously without delay
Every thirty seconds
Every two seconds
Only once when the page loads
questions.explanation: The transcript states that the client runs a setInterval, say every two seconds, to call fetch for new messages.

questions.question: What is a fundamental downside of polling more frequently, such as every 200 milliseconds?
options: It reduces latency without any trade-offs
It increases wasted work by multiplying the number of requests
It causes the server to drop connections
It makes the client unable to receive messages
questions.explanation: Polling faster reduces latency but multiplies wasted work by increasing the number of requests, as explained in the lecture.

questions.question: If a chat room is quiet and has 10,000 users polling every two seconds, what is the main inefficiency caused?
options: Serving 5,000 requests per second mostly with empty responses
Clients cannot send messages while polling
High latency in delivering messages
Server keeps too many open connections
questions.explanation: Polling every two seconds with many users leads to thousands of requests per second mostly returning no new data, causing wasted work.

questions.question: In a scenario where a client polls every two seconds, what is the average expected latency for receiving a new message?
options: Instantaneous
About one second
About two seconds
About thirty seconds
questions.explanation: Average latency is half the polling interval, so with two-second polling, it's about one second.

questions.question: Why does polling inherently involve a trade-off between latency and server load?
options: Because polling uses WebSocket frames that add overhead
Because polling cannot work through proxies
Because polling requires the server to keep many open connections
Because reducing latency by polling more frequently increases the number of wasted requests
questions.explanation: The lecture explains that polling faster lowers latency but increases wasted requests, creating a direct trade-off.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall when polling is used for a chat application expecting instant replies?
options: Latency is too high or wasted work becomes excessive, making polling unsuitable
Polling requires a complex handshake
The client cannot send messages while polling
The server cannot authenticate requests properly
questions.explanation: Polling either has high latency or high wasted work, making it the wrong tool for instant chat replies as stated in the lecture.

questions.question: What defines push-based communication in a real-time system?
options: The client sends requests at regular intervals.
The server can send data to the client without the client first requesting it.
Messages are only sent when the client refreshes the page.
The client must always initiate communication.
questions.explanation: Push-based communication means the server can initiate sending data without waiting for a client request.

questions.question: Which communication method allows both client and server to send messages at any time after a handshake?
options: Long-polling
WebSockets
HTTP refresh
Polling
questions.explanation: WebSockets upgrade a connection to a full-duplex channel allowing either side to send messages anytime.

questions.question: In a chat app needing instant updates both ways, why is push-based communication preferred over polling?
options: Because push-based communication requires no server state.
Because polling is faster and uses fewer resources.
Because polling works through every proxy on earth.
Because push-based communication reduces latency and wasted requests compared to polling.
questions.explanation: Push-based communication like WebSockets provides low latency and avoids wasted polling requests, ideal for instant updates.

questions.question: In push-based communication like WebSockets, what is the advantage over polling regarding message sending?
options: Messages require a full HTTP round trip each time
The server must wait for client requests before responding
Either client or server can send small frames at any moment after a handshake
Only the client can initiate sending messages
questions.explanation: WebSockets allow full-duplex communication where either side can send frames anytime after the handshake.

questions.question: How does push-based communication impact server resource usage compared to polling?
options: It requires no connection state on the server.
It eliminates all server resource usage.
It requires maintaining long-lived connections, increasing server state and complexity.
It uses fewer connections but more CPU for polling.
questions.explanation: Push-based communication involves long-lived connections that consume server memory and state, increasing complexity.

questions.question: What is a trade-off of push-based communication like WebSockets compared to polling?
options: Lower latency and overhead but higher server statefulness and scaling complexity.
Higher latency but less server state.
Works without any server memory.
No overhead and no statefulness.
questions.explanation: WebSockets reduce latency and overhead per message but require the server to maintain long-lived connections, complicating scaling.

questions.question: According to the course, what makes a system 'real-time' in the context of Pulse?
options: The server can tell the client something the moment it happens without the client asking first.
The system updates within milliseconds.
The server responds only to client requests.
The client refreshes the page frequently.
questions.explanation: A real-time system is defined by the server's ability to push updates to the client without a client request.

questions.question: What is NOT a key challenge in building a real-time system like Pulse?
options: Managing state of connected clients and their rooms.
Efficiently fan-out messages to many clients.
Using a stateless HTTP server that forgets clients after each response.
Scaling across multiple server processes.
questions.explanation: A stateless HTTP server is typical but insufficient for real-time; the challenge is managing state and scale.

questions.question: In a real-time chat system, why is the direction of initiation important?
options: Because the client should always initiate communication.
Because initiation direction does not affect real-time behavior.
Because the server cannot send messages without client requests.
Because the server must be able to initiate sending messages to clients to achieve real-time behavior.
questions.explanation: Real-time requires the server to initiate messages, not just respond to client requests.

questions.question: How does scaling a real-time system with multiple server processes complicate message delivery?
options: Clients connected to different servers cannot see each other's messages without additional infrastructure.
Scaling reduces latency automatically.
Scaling eliminates the need for client state.
Each server can independently handle all clients without coordination.
questions.explanation: Multiple servers require mechanisms to share client state and messages to deliver events across processes.

questions.question: Why is a system that updates only when you refresh the page not considered real-time here?
options: Because it uses WebSockets.
Because the server does not push updates unprompted; the client must ask first.
Because it uses polling.
Because the update speed is too slow.
questions.explanation: Real-time requires server-initiated updates; refreshing is client-initiated, so it is not real-time.

questions.question: What is a major challenge when running multiple server processes for a real-time system like Pulse?
options: Ensuring clients connected to different servers see each other's messages by building cross-process communication.
Reducing HTTP header sizes.
Using stateless HTTP requests.
Eliminating client reconnection.
questions.explanation: Multiple servers require mechanisms to share state and messages so clients on different servers stay synchronized.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the WebSocket handshake in the Pulse system?
options: To send polling requests at intervals.
To close the connection after each message.
To upgrade a plain HTTP connection to a persistent, full-duplex socket.
To refresh the page automatically.
questions.explanation: The handshake upgrades HTTP to a persistent WebSocket connection enabling full-duplex communication.

questions.question: How does WebSocket message overhead compare to HTTP requests in polling or long-polling?
options: WebSocket messages are always larger than polling messages.
WebSocket messages have much lower overhead, only 2 to 14 bytes of framing instead of hundreds of bytes of headers.
WebSocket messages require multiple HTTP requests per message.
WebSocket messages have more overhead due to HTTP headers.
questions.explanation: WebSocket frames have minimal framing overhead compared to full HTTP headers in polling or long-polling.

questions.question: Why does using WebSockets increase server statefulness compared to polling?
options: Because WebSockets close after each message.
Because each client connection is a long-lived socket maintained in server memory.
Because WebSockets use stateless HTTP requests.
Because WebSockets do not require a handshake.
questions.explanation: WebSockets keep persistent connections per client, increasing server memory and state requirements.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of WebSockets for a chat and presence board application like Pulse?
options: Statelessness and easy scaling.
No need for server-side client tracking.
Works without TCP connections.
Instant push in both directions with low latency and low per-message overhead.
questions.explanation: WebSockets enable real-time bidirectional communication with minimal latency and overhead, ideal for chat and presence.

questions.question: What challenge does WebSocket statefulness introduce when scaling Pulse horizontally behind a load balancer?
options: Scaling removes the need for client registry.
It reduces the number of open connections.
WebSocket connections automatically synchronize across servers.
Clients connected to different server processes cannot see each other's messages without additional cross-process communication.
questions.explanation: Because each WebSocket connection lives in one server's memory, scaling requires extra infrastructure to share messages.

questions.question: Why might libraries like ws or socket.io obscure understanding of WebSocket internals?
options: Because they only implement polling.
Because they do not support WebSocket connections.
Because they require client-side code.
Because they hide the handshake and frame parsing details that the course teaches to implement manually.
questions.explanation: The course avoids these libraries to teach the raw handshake and frame parsing so the protocol is fully understood.

questions.question: What does TCP provide between two endpoints?
options: A secure encrypted connection
A reliable, ordered, bidirectional stream of bytes
A message-based communication channel
An unordered packet delivery service
questions.explanation: TCP gives you a reliable, ordered, bidirectional stream of bytes between two endpoints.

questions.question: How does TCP identify a connection?
options: By MAC address and IP address
By source address, source port, destination address, and destination port
By port number only
By IP address only
questions.explanation: A connection is identified by four things: source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

questions.question: If a large file is piped over a TCP connection, how will the data events typically arrive?
options: In chunks of arbitrary size that do not necessarily align with the original writes
All data in a single data event
One data event per line of text
Exactly one data event per write
questions.explanation: Piping a large file will show chunks of arbitrary size, none of which line up with what you wrote, demonstrating the stream nature of TCP.

questions.question: When a WebSocket frame is received over TCP, why must the parser buffer incoming bytes?
options: Because buffering improves encryption speed
Because a frame's bytes can arrive split across multiple data events or multiple frames can arrive in one event
Because WebSocket frames are always received fully in one chunk
Because TCP guarantees one frame per data event
questions.explanation: WebSocket frame bytes can arrive split across two data events or glued together, so buffering ensures complete frames before consumption.

questions.question: What is a half-open TCP connection and why is it problematic?
options: A connection where one peer is gone but the other side does not know, causing the connection to appear alive
A connection that has been fully closed cleanly
A connection that is blocked by a firewall
A connection that uses encryption but no authentication
questions.explanation: A half-open connection occurs when a peer disappears without sending FIN or reset, leaving the other side thinking the connection is fine.

questions.question: Why is Nagle's algorithm often disabled for chat applications using TCP?
options: Because it delays small writes to batch them, increasing latency
Because it encrypts data unnecessarily
Because it causes packet loss
Because it limits the number of concurrent connections
questions.explanation: Nagle's algorithm delays small writes to batch them, which increases latency, so disabling it improves responsiveness for chat apps.

questions.question: What does the FIN bit in a WebSocket frame indicate?
options: That the frame is a continuation
That this is the final fragment of a message
That the frame is masked
That the frame contains a ping
questions.explanation: The FIN bit indicates this frame is the final fragment of a message.

questions.question: What opcode value corresponds to a text frame in WebSocket?
questions.explanation: Opcode 0x1 means a text frame.

questions.question: If a WebSocket frame's payload length byte is 126, how is the actual payload length determined?
options: It is the same as the MASK bit
It is exactly 126 bytes
It is stored in the next eight bytes as a 64-bit integer
It is stored in the next two bytes as a big-endian unsigned 16-bit integer
questions.explanation: If length is 126, the real length is in the next two bytes as a big-endian unsigned 16-bit integer.

questions.question: Why must client-to-server WebSocket frames be masked?
options: To compress the payload
To authenticate the client
To encrypt the data for security
To prevent a malicious page from crafting bytes that a transparent proxy might mistake for an HTTP response
questions.explanation: Masking prevents cache-poisoning attacks by stopping malicious pages from crafting bytes that look like HTTP responses to proxies.

questions.question: What should a server do if it receives an unmasked frame from a client?
options: Accept the frame normally
Ignore the mask bit
Close the connection with a protocol error
Mask it and process
questions.explanation: The RFC requires the server to close the connection with a protocol error if it receives an unmasked client frame.

questions.question: Why is XOR used with the masking key when unmasking a WebSocket payload?
options: Because XOR generates a checksum
Because XOR is its own inverse, so the same operation masks and unmasks
Because XOR compresses the data
Because XOR encrypts the payload
questions.explanation: XOR is its own inverse, so applying it again with the same key unmasks the payload.

questions.question: Which header indicates that a client wants to upgrade an HTTP connection to a WebSocket?
options: Sec-WebSocket-Version: 12
Content-Type: websocket
Connection: close
Upgrade: websocket
questions.explanation: The header `Upgrade: websocket` signals the client's request to upgrade to a WebSocket connection.

questions.question: What is the significance of the double CRLF sequence in the WebSocket upgrade request?
options: It starts the WebSocket payload
It marks the end of the HTTP header section
It signals a protocol error
It indicates the connection should be closed
questions.explanation:
The double CRLF sequence (`

`) marks the end of the HTTP headers in the upgrade request.

questions.question: Why does the server compute the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header during handshake?
options: To negotiate subprotocols
To encrypt the WebSocket connection
