questions.question: What causes bugs related to confusion between lexical and dynamic scope?
options: Using closures
Using let instead of var
Using global variables
Expecting variables to be visible based on the caller rather than the code location
questions.explanation: Confusing lexical and dynamic scope causes bugs because JavaScript uses lexical scope, not dynamic.
questions.lecture: 2.1 - Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain

questions.question: Why does a function defined inside another function retain access to the outer function's variables even after the outer function returns?
options: Because the inner function carries a reference to the scope object created when it was defined, which lives on the heap
Because the variables are copied into the inner function's local scope
Because the call stack keeps the outer function's frame alive until all inner functions finish
Because JavaScript dynamically looks up variables from the caller's scope

questions.question: How does the scope chain work when looking up a variable?
options: It checks child scopes first
It checks only the global scope
It checks the current scope's bindings, then recursively checks parent scopes
It checks only the current scope

questions.question: What happens if a variable is not found in any scope during lookup?
options: Undefined is returned
A ReferenceError is thrown
The variable is created globally

questions.question: Why can't a scope lookup find a variable declared in a child scope?
options: Because variables are global
Because child scopes are merged

questions.question: How does the scope chain explain why a variable declared in a child scope is not accessible from the parent?
options: Because scope links only point outward from child to parent, not inward
Because child scopes are merged with parents
Because parent scopes shadow child scopes
Because variables are copied up

questions.question: When looking up a variable in a nested scope, what is the order in which scopes are searched?

Start from the current scope and recursively check each parent scope outward until found or error
Check sibling scopes before the parent scope
Start from the global scope and check inward to the current scope

questions.question: What happens if you try to access a let variable before its declaration line runs?

Because let variables are hoisted as functions
Because typeof only works on undeclared variables, not declared ones

questions.question: Why is step four of the new operator process (using the constructor's returned object if any) rarely used?

questions.question: What can go wrong if you call a constructor function without new in sloppy mode?

questions.question: What is the correct order of steps the new operator follows when called with a constructor function?

questions.question: How does the new binding rule affect this when a function is called with new?

this is set to undefined
this is set to a fresh new object created by new

questions.question: Why does bind override implicit binding when both apply?

Because explicit binding has higher priority than implicit binding
Because new binding is ignored when bind is used
questions.explanation: Explicit binding (bind) beats implicit binding due to the priority order.

questions.question: What is the value of this when a plain function is called without any object or new?
options: The global object or undefined in strict mode
The object before the dot
The function's prototype
A new empty object

questions.question: What does the prototype link (__proto__) in JavaScript objects represent?

An internal link to another object from which properties are inherited
A direct reference to the constructor function itself
A list of all methods defined on the object

questions.question: When using class syntax, how is inheritance between classes established?

Dog.prototype.constructor === Animal
Dog.__proto__ === Animal.prototype

The property is set on the prototype object
The property is set directly on the object, not on its prototype
The property is copied to all objects in the chain

questions.question: If object A's prototype is object B, and you access a method not on A, what happens?

JavaScript copies the method from B to A
JavaScript throws a ReferenceError
JavaScript looks for the method on A's constructor

options: Because all instances share one copy of inherited methods rather than each having their own copy
Because it stores methods in a separate memory pool
Because methods are copied only when accessed
Because it caches methods on each instance
questions.explanation: Delegation means all instances share one copy of inherited methods, saving memory compared to copying methods to each instance.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when assigning properties in a prototype chain?

Writing a property updates all objects in the chain
Writing a property deletes the prototype's property
Writing a property shadows the prototype's property, leading to unexpected behavior

questions.question: Why is prototype delegation described as a delegation chain rather than a copy?
options: Because the chain copies methods lazily on first access
Because property lookups delegate to prototypes at runtime without copying properties
Because delegation copies methods but not properties
Because properties are copied only once during object creation
questions.explanation: Objects do not copy properties from their prototype; they delegate lookups to it at runtime, forming a delegation chain.

questions.question: What happens during prototype lookup when a property is accessed on an object?

JavaScript only checks the object's own properties
JavaScript copies the property from the prototype to the object
JavaScript searches the object first, then walks up the prototype chain until found or null

questions.question: Where is the toString method found when called on an empty object with no such own property?

On Array.prototype
On the object's constructor function

questions.question: What does an inline cache store at a property access site in V8?

The hidden class and offset of the property

questions.question: What is the state called when an inline cache has only ever seen one hidden class at a property access site?

Megamorphic

questions.question: If a function is called with objects of five different shapes at a property access site, what inline cache state does it enter?

Megamorphic
Polymorphic

questions.question: Why is code that only sees one hidden class at a property access site faster than code that sees many?
options: Because the optimizing compiler can inline and optimize monomorphic sites best
Because it uses dictionary mode
Because it performs a full prototype walk
Because it disables inline caches
questions.explanation: Monomorphic sites allow the compiler to bake in assumptions about the shape, enabling better optimization.

questions.question: What happens to the inline cache when it grows beyond four different hidden classes at a site?

It becomes megamorphic and stops caching
It converts to dictionary mode
It merges all shapes into one
questions.explanation: When the cache grows beyond four entries, it becomes megamorphic, stops caching, and uses a shared global lookup.

questions.question: What is a trade-off of megamorphic inline caches compared to monomorphic ones?

Megamorphic caches are significantly slower due to fallback to global lookup tables
Megamorphic caches are faster because they cache more shapes
questions.explanation: Megamorphic caches fall back to slower global lookup tables, making them significantly slower than monomorphic caches.

questions.question: What does 'monomorphic' mean in the context of inline caches?
options: The object is in dictionary mode
The cache has seen only one hidden class at a property access site
The cache is disabled
The cache has seen many different hidden classes
questions.explanation: Monomorphic means the inline cache has seen only one hidden class, enabling the fastest access.

questions.question: What does it mean when an inline cache is described as 'monomorphic'?
options: The cache does not store any hidden class information and performs generic lookups.
The cache has seen two to four different hidden classes and stores them in a list.
The cache has seen more than four hidden classes and falls back to a global lookup table.
The cache has only ever seen one hidden class at a property access site.
questions.explanation: An inline cache is monomorphic if it has only ever seen one hidden class at a property access site, making it the fastest state.

questions.question: What is the difference between polymorphic and megamorphic inline caches?
options: Polymorphic caches handle 2-4 shapes, megamorphic caches handle more than 4 and fallback to slower lookup
Polymorphic caches handle one shape, megamorphic caches handle two shapes
Polymorphic caches are slower than megamorphic caches
Polymorphic caches disable caching, megamorphic caches enable caching
questions.explanation: Polymorphic caches handle a few shapes with a short list, megamorphic caches handle many shapes and use a slower global lookup.

questions.question: Why is it beneficial to keep functions monomorphic by passing objects of the same kind?

Because it forces megamorphic state
Because it increases dictionary mode usage
Because it disables inline caches
questions.explanation: Monomorphic inline caches allow the compiler to optimize code by baking in assumptions about object shapes.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of a function handling many different object kinds in terms of inline cache state?

It can become megamorphic, causing slower property access
It disables hidden classes

Because it moves the function to the macrotask queue.

questions.question: How can layered debugging help when encountering a new confusing bug?
options: By ignoring the bug and hoping it resolves
By only using browser devtools without understanding layers
By asking which layer it lives in and applying the corresponding mental model
By rewriting the entire program from scratch

Avoid reading the ECMAScript specification
Only read high-level tutorials
Stop learning because the model is complete

questions.question: What is a pitfall when debugging without layered mental models?
options: Ignoring all runtime errors
Misattributing bugs to the wrong layer and wasting time
Using only one debugger tool
Fixing bugs too quickly

questions.question: When debugging a complex bug that spans multiple layers, what is a key challenge of layered debugging that requires careful reasoning?
options: Rewriting the entire program to isolate the bug in a single layer.
Identifying which layer is responsible for each symptom and understanding how layers interact to cause the bug.
Using only console logs without models or simulations.
Ignoring timing issues and focusing only on scope problems.

questions.question: What does the run-to-completion rule state about macrotasks like setTimeout callbacks?
options: They run before microtasks
They can preempt the current task
They run only after the current script task finishes and the stack is empty
They run immediately inside the loop

Because the log runs before any setTimeout callback has executed due to run-to-completion
Because results is never updated

Assuming data is ready immediately after scheduling callbacks, causing empty or stale reads

questions.question: What type of HTTP request initiates a WebSocket connection?
options: PUT
POST
GET
DELETE
questions.explanation: A WebSocket connection begins with a regular HTTP GET request including the Upgrade: websocket header.

questions.question: Which header must be included in the initial HTTP request to ask the server to switch to a WebSocket connection?
options: Accept-Encoding: gzip
Content-Type: application/json
Connection: close
Upgrade: websocket
questions.explanation: The client includes the Upgrade: websocket header to request the server to upgrade the HTTP connection to a WebSocket.

questions.question: You inspect the very first request a browser sends when it opens a WebSocket. Which description matches what the lecture says you'll see?
options: An HTTP GET carrying an Upgrade: websocket header and a randomly generated, base64-encoded Sec-WebSocket-Key header
An HTTP POST whose body already contains the first WebSocket frame
An HTTP GET carrying a Sec-WebSocket-Accept header that the browser computed with SHA-1
A raw frame sent straight to the ws:// URL with no HTTP headers at all
questions.explanation: The handshake begins as a regular HTTP GET that includes Upgrade: websocket and a Sec-WebSocket-Key, a randomly generated base64-encoded value; Sec-WebSocket-Accept is the server's response header.

questions.question: In a scenario where a WebSocket URL starts with ws://, what protocol does the initial handshake use?
options: FTP
HTTPS
HTTP
SMTP
questions.explanation: The initial handshake for a WebSocket connection uses HTTP even if the URL starts with ws://.

questions.question: A WebSocket URL starts with ws:// or wss://, yet the very first thing the browser sends is an HTTP GET request. Why?
options: The GET downloads a WebSocket protocol handler, after which the browser opens a new TCP connection to the ws:// URL
ws:// and wss:// are aliases for http:// and https://, so the connection stays plain HTTP request-response
The browser first fetches its Sec-WebSocket-Key from the server over HTTP, then connects separately over ws://
The handshake itself travels over HTTP: the GET carries Upgrade: websocket, asking the server to upgrade that same HTTP connection to a persistent WebSocket connection
questions.explanation: The lecture explains that the handshake starts as a regular HTTP GET with an Upgrade: websocket header — the browser asks the server to upgrade this HTTP connection — which is why ws:// URLs still begin with an HTTP handshake.

questions.question: What could be a pitfall if a proxy server does not support the Upgrade: websocket header in the initial HTTP request?
options: The server will ignore the header and accept the connection
The WebSocket connection will silently downgrade to HTTP/2
The client will retry with a POST request
The handshake will fail and the connection won't upgrade
questions.explanation: If a proxy does not support Upgrade: websocket, the handshake fails and the connection cannot upgrade to WebSocket.

questions.question: What HTTP status code does the server send to confirm it is switching protocols to WebSocket?
options: 500 Internal Server Error
404 Not Found
101 Switching Protocols
200 OK
questions.explanation: The server responds with 101 Switching Protocols to confirm the upgrade to WebSocket.

questions.question: What header does the server send in response to the Sec-WebSocket-Key to confirm the handshake?
options: Upgrade
Connection
Sec-WebSocket-Key
Sec-WebSocket-Accept
questions.explanation: The server sends Sec-WebSocket-Accept derived from the client's key to confirm the handshake.

questions.question: If a client receives a Sec-WebSocket-Accept header that does not match the expected value, what should it do?
options: Reject the connection as invalid
Proceed with the connection
Retry the handshake
Ignore the header and send data
questions.explanation: The client verifies the Sec-WebSocket-Accept to ensure it's talking to a genuine server and rejects invalid responses.

questions.question: After the handshake completes, what kind of communication does the WebSocket connection support?
options: Client-to-server requests only
Full-duplex communication in both directions
Server-to-client responses only
Unidirectional broadcast from server
questions.explanation: Once the handshake completes, the connection is full-duplex allowing both sides to send frames anytime.

questions.question: Why does the server concatenate a fixed GUID string to the Sec-WebSocket-Key before hashing it?
options: To convert the key to lowercase
To create a unique accept token for validation
To compress the key for faster transmission
To encrypt the key for security
questions.explanation: The server concatenates a fixed GUID to the key and hashes it to create a unique Sec-WebSocket-Accept for validation.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall if a client does not verify the Sec-WebSocket-Accept header properly?
options: The connection might be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks
The handshake will automatically retry
The client will send duplicate frames
The server will close the connection immediately
questions.explanation: Not verifying Sec-WebSocket-Accept can cause the client to connect to a misconfigured proxy or attacker, risking security.

questions.question: In long-polling, what does the server do with the client's HTTP request?
options: Sends a 404 error
Responds immediately with cached data
Holds the request open until data is available
Closes the connection immediately
questions.explanation: The server deliberately holds the client's request open until new data is available in long-polling.

questions.question: What happens immediately after the server responds to a long-polling request with data?
options: The client closes the connection
The server upgrades the connection to WebSocket
The client stops requesting data
The client sends another request to wait for more data
questions.explanation: After receiving data, the client instantly sends another request to simulate a continuous connection.

questions.question: If a client wants to simulate a push notification using HTTP but cannot use WebSockets, which method should it use?
options: HTTP/2 Server Push
Long-polling
FTP
Polling
questions.explanation: Long-polling simulates push by holding requests open and immediately re-requesting after a response.

questions.question: How does long-polling affect server resource usage compared to WebSockets in a high-frequency update scenario?
options: It uses the same resources as WebSockets
It reduces CPU usage by caching responses
It uses fewer resources because connections close quickly
It uses more resources due to repeated HTTP requests
questions.explanation: Long-polling uses more resources because each message requires a full HTTP request and response cycle.

questions.question: What is a drawback of long-polling related to the timing of messages?
options: The server can push data without client requests
There is a gap between responses during client reconnects
Messages are sent in both directions simultaneously
Messages are delivered instantly without delay
questions.explanation: Long-polling has a gap between responses where the client reconnects, causing latency.

questions.question: Why might long-polling fail or perform poorly behind some proxies?
options: Proxies upgrade the connection to WebSocket automatically
Proxies cache all long-polling responses
Proxies block all HTTP GET requests
Proxies may close idle connections before data arrives
questions.explanation: Some proxies close idle connections held open by long-polling, disrupting the simulated push mechanism.

questions.question: Which method uses a single long-lived full-duplex connection with minimal framing overhead?
options: Long-polling
WebSocket
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive
Polling
questions.explanation: WebSocket uses one long-lived full-duplex connection with tiny framing overhead after the handshake.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of long-polling compared to WebSockets in terms of HTTP requests?
options: Long-polling sends no HTTP requests
Long-polling uses UDP packets instead of HTTP
Long-polling uses a single HTTP request for all messages
Long-polling sends one HTTP request per message
questions.explanation: Long-polling sends a full HTTP request for each message, unlike WebSocket's persistent connection.

questions.question: In a chat application with frequent bidirectional messages, which method is more efficient and why?
options: WebSocket, because it uses multiple TCP connections
Long-polling, because it works through old proxies
Long-polling, because it uses simple HTTP requests
WebSocket, because it maintains a single full-duplex connection with low overhead
questions.explanation: WebSocket is more efficient for frequent bidirectional traffic due to its single persistent connection and low framing overhead.

questions.question: Why might long-polling still be used despite WebSockets' efficiency advantages?
options: It uses less bandwidth for high-frequency updates
It has lower latency than WebSockets
It is simpler and works through old proxies
It supports full-duplex communication
questions.explanation: Long-polling is simpler and compatible with old proxies, making it suitable for some use cases.

questions.question: What is a trade-off when choosing long-polling over WebSockets for real-time updates?
options: Long-polling encrypts data by default while WebSockets do not
Long-polling requires multiple HTTP requests causing overhead and reconnect gaps
Long-polling has lower overhead but higher latency
Long-polling supports full-duplex communication unlike WebSockets
questions.explanation: Long-polling pays the overhead of repeated HTTP requests and has gaps during reconnects, unlike WebSockets.

questions.question: What might happen if a WebSocket connection drops and the client falls back to long-polling?
options: The client will gain full-duplex communication
The client will experience increased latency and overhead due to reconnects
The client will stop receiving updates
The server will close all connections immediately
questions.explanation: Falling back to long-polling increases overhead and latency because of repeated HTTP requests and reconnect gaps.

questions.question: In the HTTP request-response contract, who initiates the communication?
options: Both client and server initiate simultaneously
Neither initiates; communication is automatic
The server initiates the request
The client initiates the request
questions.explanation: HTTP is a request and response protocol where the client speaks first and the server answers.

questions.question: What does the server do after sending a response in the HTTP request-response model?
options: It closes the conversation and waits for the next request
It immediately sends a follow-up request
It keeps the connection open indefinitely
It pushes new data to the client spontaneously
questions.explanation: After the server responds, the conversation is over; the server cannot push data out of the blue.

questions.question: If a client wants to receive live updates but HTTP only allows server responses to client requests, which technique can simulate live updates by asking repeatedly?
options: Short polling
WebSockets
Server-Sent Events
Long-polling
questions.explanation: Short polling involves the client repeatedly asking the server for updates to simulate live data.

questions.question: How does long-polling differ from short polling in terms of server response timing?
options: The client sends multiple requests simultaneously
The server responds immediately with the current data
The server upgrades the connection to WebSocket
The server holds the request open until it has new data
questions.explanation: Long-polling keeps the request open until the server has new data, unlike short polling which responds immediately.

questions.question: Why is it important to use a version number in the polling requests?
options: To allow the server to remember the client
To reduce the size of the JSON response
To enable the server to push data without requests
To avoid losing updates that happen between requests
questions.explanation: The version number helps the client detect if it is behind and ensures no updates are lost between requests.

questions.question: What is a key limitation of the HTTP request-response contract that all real-time techniques in this course must work around?
options: The server cannot send data without a client request
The client cannot send multiple requests simultaneously
HTTP connections are always encrypted
HTTP does not support JSON data
questions.explanation: HTTP requires the client to initiate requests; the server cannot push data spontaneously.

questions.question: What is the simplest way to update a live scoreboard using HTTP?
options: Long-polling by holding requests open
Short polling by asking the server every second
Using Server-Sent Events to stream data
Using WebSockets for a full-duplex connection
questions.explanation: Short polling is the simplest approach where the client asks the server every second for updates.

questions.question: Why does short polling waste server resources when updates are infrequent?
options: Because the server upgrades every request to WebSocket
Because the client cannot parse JSON efficiently
Because many requests return unchanged data
Because the server must keep connections open
questions.explanation: Short polling sends many requests that often return identical data, causing wasted bandwidth and server load.

questions.question: If the scoreboard simulator updates every 3 seconds, what is the average delay a user experiences with short polling set to 1 second intervals?
options: About half a second delay on average
About 1.5 seconds delay on average
No delay at all
Exactly 3 seconds delay
questions.explanation: With a 1 second polling interval, updates can appear anywhere from 0 to 1 second late, averaging half a second delay.

questions.question: What happens to server load if you reduce the short polling interval from 1 second to 100 milliseconds?
options: Server load stays the same as updates are infrequent
Server load decreases due to caching
Server load decreases because requests are smaller
Server load increases tenfold due to more frequent requests
questions.explanation: Reducing the interval by a factor of ten increases the number of requests tenfold, raising server load.

questions.question: What is the fundamental trade-off in short polling?
options: Between JSON size and request headers
Between update freshness and resource cost
Between server memory and client CPU
Between HTTP version and browser support
questions.explanation: Short polling ties freshness and cost together; improving one increases the other.

questions.question: Why does short polling not save server work even when using a version number to return 204 status for no changes?
options: Because the server still processes every request fully
Because the version number resets frequently
Because the client ignores the 204 status
Because 204 responses are larger than JSON
questions.explanation: Even with 204 responses, the server must handle each request, so the processing cost remains.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'version' field in the matchState object?
options: To track changes and help clients detect updates
To identify the home team
To count the number of goals scored
To store the current minute of the match
questions.explanation: The version number increments on every change and helps clients know if they have the latest state.

questions.question: How does the server respond when the client's 'since' query parameter equals the current version?
options: It sends a 204 No Content response
It closes the connection without response
It sends the full matchState JSON
It upgrades to a WebSocket connection
questions.explanation: If the client is up to date, the server responds with 204 to indicate no new data.

questions.question: In long-polling, how does the server use the version number to decide when to respond immediately?
options: If the server's version is less than the client's 'since' value, respond immediately
The version number is ignored in long-polling
If the server's version is greater than the client's 'since' value, respond immediately
If the server's version equals the client's 'since' value, respond immediately
questions.explanation: The server compares versions and responds immediately if the client is behind.

questions.question: What problem does the version number help solve during the gap between long-polling requests?
options: It enables multiplexing of connections
It prevents loss of updates that occur between requests
It reduces the size of the HTTP headers
It allows the server to push data spontaneously
questions.explanation: The version number ensures updates are not missed during the small gap when no request is parked.

questions.question: What could happen if you did not use a version number with long-polling?
options: Updates might be lost during the gap between requests
The connection would upgrade to WebSocket automatically
The server would respond with errors
The client would receive duplicate updates
questions.explanation: Without the version number, events occurring between requests could be missed.

questions.question: Why is the version number described as the 'hero' in the polling and long-polling implementations?
options: Because it enables reliable detection of changes despite stateless HTTP
Because it stores the full match state on the client
Because it automatically upgrades the connection to WebSocket
Because it reduces the size of JSON responses dramatically
questions.explanation: The version number allows clients to detect if they have missed updates in a stateless protocol.

questions.question: What HTTP status code does a server send to indicate it agrees to switch protocols?

questions.question: Why does the WebSocket protocol start as an HTTP request instead of opening a new port?
options: Because browsers do not support new ports
Because WebSocket requires HTTP cookies to function
Because ports 80 and 443 are almost always open and allow WebSocket traffic through firewalls
Because HTTP is faster than opening a new port
questions.explanation: Starting as HTTP allows WebSocket connections to pass through existing infrastructure and firewalls that allow ports 80 and 443.

questions.question: If a proxy or load balancer removes the Upgrade or Connection headers, what is the likely effect on a WebSocket connection?

The WebSocket connection will fail to establish
The connection will fall back to HTTP polling
The connection will upgrade successfully

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Sec-WebSocket-Key and Sec-WebSocket-Accept headers in the WebSocket handshake?
options: To authenticate the client
To prove the server understands the WebSocket protocol and prevent cached HTTP responses
To encrypt the WebSocket connection
To negotiate the WebSocket version
questions.explanation: These headers confirm the server understands the protocol and prevent mistaken cached HTTP responses.

questions.question: Why is the Upgrade request considered a request and not a command in HTTP?
options: Because the server can refuse or ignore the upgrade request
Because it opens a new TCP connection
Because it always results in an upgrade
Because it requires authentication
questions.explanation: The server may ignore or refuse the upgrade request, so it's a request, not a command.

questions.question: Which event does the Node.js HTTP server emit when it receives an Upgrade request?
options: handshake
upgrade
request
connection

questions.question: What WebSocket API event is triggered when a message is received from the server in the browser?
options: close
message
error
open

questions.question: If you want to send data over a WebSocket in the browser, which readyState must the socket be in?
options: CONNECTING (0)
CLOSING (2)
CLOSED (3)
OPEN (1)

questions.question: What is the purpose of the WebSocketServer class from the 'ws' package in Node.js?
options: To parse raw WebSocket frames manually
To handle WebSocket connections and handshakes on top of an HTTP server
To serve static files over HTTP
To proxy HTTP requests
questions.explanation: WebSocketServer manages WebSocket handshakes and connections attached to an HTTP server.

questions.question: Why does the WebSocket API's error event provide almost no detail?
options: To avoid leaking sensitive information
Because the protocol does not support error reporting
Because errors are always fatal
Because errors are rare
questions.explanation: The error event carries little detail on purpose to avoid leaking sensitive info.

questions.question: What close code indicates a normal WebSocket closure?
questions.explanation: Code 1000 means normal closure, while 1006 means abnormal closure without a close frame.

questions.question: What does the FIN bit in a WebSocket frame indicate?
options: Whether the frame is masked
The opcode type of the frame
Whether this frame is the final fragment of a message
The payload length
questions.explanation: The FIN bit signals if this is the last fragment of a fragmented message.

questions.question: Which opcode represents a text frame in a WebSocket message?
questions.explanation: Opcode 0x1 is used for text frames carrying UTF-8 payloads.

questions.question: If a WebSocket frame's payload length is 126, what does that mean for the frame format?
options: The frame is invalid
The payload length is exactly 126 bytes
The next eight bytes hold the 64-bit payload length
The next two bytes hold the actual 16-bit payload length
questions.explanation: A length of 126 means the next two bytes specify the real 16-bit length.

questions.question: Why must every frame sent from the browser to the server be masked?
options: To authenticate the client
To prevent proxies from confusing WebSocket payloads with HTTP requests
To encrypt the payload
To compress the data
questions.explanation: Masking prevents badly behaved proxies from mistaking payloads for HTTP requests.

questions.question: What is the maximum payload size for control frames like ping and pong in WebSocket?
options: 125 bytes
Unlimited
64 bytes
256 bytes
questions.explanation: Control frames are limited to at most 125 bytes and cannot be fragmented.

questions.question: What could go wrong if a WebSocket frame from the browser was not masked?
options: The server would reject the frame
Proxies might cache or misinterpret the frame as an HTTP request, causing errors
The client would disconnect immediately
The frame would be encrypted improperly
questions.explanation: Without masking, proxies could confuse frames with HTTP requests and cause caching issues.

questions.question: What does Server-Sent Events (SSE) use to deliver messages from the server to the browser?

Repeated HTTP POST requests from the client
A WebSocket full-duplex connection
A persistent HTTP response that never finishes and sends text events

questions.question: Which built-in browser class is used to receive Server-Sent Events?

XMLHttpRequest
WebSocket
Fetch API

questions.question: If a scoreboard app only needs to receive occasional updates from the server and never sends data back, which transport is most suitable?

Server-Sent Events (SSE)
WebSockets
Long-polling
questions.explanation: SSE fits one-way, occasional updates with automatic reconnect and less complexity than WebSockets.

questions.question: How does SSE handle reconnection and missed messages after a network drop?
options: The server closes the connection and the client restarts a new one without state
SSE does not support automatic reconnection
The browser sends a Last-Event-ID header with the last received message ID, allowing the server to resend missed events
The client must manually reconnect and request missing messages
questions.explanation: SSE automatically reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID header so the server can send any missed messages.
questions.lecture: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of using SSE on HTTP/1.1 with many open tabs?
options: Browsers limit simultaneous connections per domain to about six, so multiple SSE tabs can starve other requests
SSE cannot send JSON data
SSE messages can be lost if the server buffers too much data
SSE requires a WebSocket upgrade handshake which may fail
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 limits about six simultaneous connections per domain, so many SSE tabs can block other requests.
questions.lecture: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP

questions.question: Why might SSE be preferred over WebSockets for features like notifications or live feeds?
options: SSE is simpler, uses plain HTTP without upgrade, and includes built-in reconnect with catch-up
SSE supports bidirectional communication, unlike WebSockets
WebSockets cannot send text messages
WebSockets require no server configuration
questions.explanation: SSE offers simpler implementation with automatic reconnect and no upgrade needed, ideal for mostly server-to-client flows.
questions.lecture: 3.2 - Server-Sent Events: One-Way Push over HTTP

questions.question: What metric did the lecture measure to compare transports that counts the data sent over the network?

Number of open connections
Bytes on the wire
Latency from event to screen

Short polling
Server-Sent Events

questions.question: In a scenario with one client receiving updates every three seconds, which transport had latency closest to zero milliseconds locally?

Long-polling, SSE, and WebSockets
WebSockets only
Short polling and long-polling
questions.explanation: Long-polling, SSE, and WebSockets all showed latency within a few milliseconds locally, unlike short polling.

questions.question: How does the cost of open connections compare between short polling and long-lived connections like SSE or WebSockets on the server?
options: WebSockets use no memory on the server
Held connections cost memory for SSE and WebSockets; short polling costs CPU for repeated requests
SSE connections use more CPU than short polling
Short polling uses less CPU and memory than SSE
questions.explanation: Held connections consume memory for SSE and WebSockets, while short polling uses CPU to handle each request.

questions.question: Why is it important to measure transport performance rather than just rely on assumptions?
options: Because all transports perform the same
Because measurement is not needed if the API is popular
Because measurement only matters for WebSockets
Because performance claims without measurement are just opinions
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes that unmeasured performance claims are opinions, so measuring is an engineering habit.

questions.question: What trade-off does the lecture highlight when choosing between long-polling and WebSockets?
options: Long-polling supports bidirectional communication, WebSockets do not
Long-polling requires no headers, WebSockets require many headers
WebSockets are always better and simpler than long-polling
Long-polling works everywhere with HTTP but is less efficient; WebSockets are efficient but need infrastructure support
questions.explanation: Long-polling uses plain HTTP and works through proxies but is less efficient; WebSockets need upgrade support but are more efficient.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of WebSockets over long-polling for real-time applications?
options: Uses only HTTP/1.1 without upgrades
No need for any server configuration
A single long-lived full-duplex TCP connection with low framing overhead
Automatic reconnection and message catch-up built-in
questions.explanation: WebSockets create a persistent full-duplex connection after an HTTP Upgrade, reducing overhead per message.

questions.question: Before WebSockets were widely supported, how did developers simulate push notifications in browsers?
options: Using Server-Sent Events
Using long-polling with held HTTP requests
Using WebRTC
Using WebSocket polyfills
questions.explanation: Long-polling was the common technique before WebSockets to simulate server push over HTTP.

questions.question: If a multiplayer game requires sending updates sixty times per second in both directions, which transport is recommended?
options: Server-Sent Events
Short polling
WebSockets
Long-polling
questions.explanation: WebSockets support high-frequency, bidirectional traffic efficiently, unlike SSE or polling.

questions.question: Why might a developer choose long-polling over WebSockets despite WebSockets being more efficient?
options: Long-polling works through old proxies and requires no special server configuration
Long-polling supports bidirectional communication better
Long-polling uses less bandwidth for high-frequency updates
Long-polling requires no reconnect logic
questions.explanation: Long-polling works with any HTTP infrastructure and proxies without needing WebSocket upgrade support.

questions.question: What common mistake do developers make when adopting WebSockets for their applications?
options: Using WebSockets without any reconnect logic
Replacing all communication with WebSockets even for rare messages, increasing complexity unnecessarily
Using WebSockets only for server-to-client one-way push
Not using WebSockets for high-frequency bidirectional traffic
questions.explanation: Developers sometimes use WebSockets for infrequent messages, inheriting complexity like reconnects and scaling unnecessarily.

questions.question: What infrastructure changes are often required to support WebSockets in production?
options: Configuring load balancers for Upgrade handshake and sticky routing or shared message layers
No changes are needed since WebSockets use plain HTTP
Replacing TCP with UDP
Disabling TLS to allow WebSocket connections
questions.explanation: WebSockets require load balancers to support the Upgrade handshake and sticky sessions or shared state for scaling.

questions.question: What happens when a WebSocket connection closes and you try to use the same WebSocket object again?
options: The WebSocket buffers messages until the connection is restored
The WebSocket object cannot be reopened and is finished
The WebSocket sends a ping to check the connection
The WebSocket automatically reconnects
questions.explanation: A closed WebSocket is finished and cannot be reopened, so to reconnect you must create a new WebSocket object.

questions.question: Why does a fixed retry interval for reconnecting WebSocket clients cause a thundering herd problem?
options: Clients retry in synchronized intervals causing server overload
Clients retry at increasing intervals causing overload
Clients never retry causing permanent disconnection
Clients send too many ping messages causing congestion
questions.explanation: A fixed retry interval causes all clients to retry simultaneously, overwhelming the server with many handshakes at once.

questions.question: If a server is down for a long time and many clients retry every second, how does exponential backoff help?
options: It forces clients to send ping messages before retrying
It makes clients retry faster to restore connection quickly
It spreads out retries by increasing wait times between attempts
It stops clients from retrying to reduce server load
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff increases the wait time after each failed attempt, reducing load by spreading retries over time.

questions.question: How would you modify a reconnect strategy to avoid all clients retrying at the exact same time?
options: Send ping messages before reconnecting
Add jitter by randomizing the retry delay
Retry immediately without waiting
Use a fixed interval retry without changes
questions.explanation: Adding jitter randomizes retry delays so clients do not retry in lockstep, preventing synchronized retries.

questions.question: What is a potential problem if you do not reset the retry attempt counter after a successful WebSocket connection?
options: The client will flood the server with retries
The client will always wait the maximum delay before retrying
The client will close the connection immediately
The client will never retry after a failure
questions.explanation: Without resetting attempts, the client retains the high retry delay and waits the maximum time even after a successful connection.

questions.question: Why is it important for the reconnect protocol to send the last seen version or full state after reconnecting?
options: To ensure the client has the complete and current state after disconnection
To reduce the number of reconnection attempts
To avoid sending any data after reconnecting
To close the connection immediately after reconnecting
questions.explanation: Sending the last seen version or full state ensures the client receives all updates missed during disconnection.

questions.question: What does the `bufferedAmount` property on a WebSocket represent?
options: The number of active WebSocket connections
The number of messages received but not processed
The number of bytes passed to send but not yet transmitted
The number of bytes sent and acknowledged by the network
questions.explanation: `bufferedAmount` indicates how many bytes have been passed to send but have not yet been transmitted to the network.

questions.question: In a stress test where the server sends updates faster than the client can process, what happens to `bufferedAmount`?
options: It decreases steadily
It stays near zero
It climbs steadily for slow clients
It resets to zero after each message
questions.explanation: When the client is slow, `bufferedAmount` climbs as messages queue up waiting to be sent.

questions.question: If a client’s `bufferedAmount` exceeds 64 KB, what is a simple server-side strategy to handle this?
options: Close the client connection immediately
Send more messages to catch up
Skip sending messages to that client temporarily
Reset the client’s buffer manually
questions.explanation: Skipping messages when `bufferedAmount` is high prevents making the client’s backlog worse and uses load shedding.

questions.question: How should you handle backpressure for event streams where every message matters, such as chat lines?
options: Send only ping messages
Skip messages when the buffer is full
Pause the producer or queue messages with limits
Ignore backpressure and keep sending
questions.explanation: For event streams, you must slow the producer or queue messages with limits to avoid losing important events.

questions.question: What is a recommended action when a client is hopelessly slow and causes memory pressure due to backpressure?
options: Ignore the problem and keep sending
Send duplicate messages to the client
Increase the buffer size indefinitely
Disconnect the client to free resources
questions.explanation: Disconnecting a slow client prevents it from consuming excessive memory shared by all clients.

questions.question: Why does the WebSocket API provide the `bufferedAmount` property instead of exposing TCP flow control directly?
options: Because WebSocket runs over UDP
Because `bufferedAmount` is easier to implement
Because TCP flow control is unreliable
Because TCP flow control is built-in but not exposed to JavaScript
questions.explanation: TCP has built-in flow control but it is not exposed directly to JavaScript, so `bufferedAmount` is provided as a proxy.

questions.question: What is exponential backoff in the context of reconnecting WebSocket clients?
options: Retrying at a fixed interval regardless of failures
Waiting longer after each failed reconnect attempt
Sending ping messages before reconnecting
Retrying immediately after a failure
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff means increasing the wait time after each failed reconnect attempt, typically doubling it.

questions.question: Why is jitter added to exponential backoff delays?
options: To speed up retries
To add randomness and spread out retries
To disable retries after a limit
To synchronize clients' retries
questions.explanation: Jitter adds randomness to retry delays to prevent clients from retrying simultaneously and causing a thundering herd.

questions.question: If a client has failed to reconnect 3 times, what would be the approximate maximum delay before the next attempt using exponential backoff starting at 1 second?
options: 8 seconds
4 seconds
16 seconds
32 seconds
questions.explanation: After 3 failed attempts, delay doubles each time: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, so the 4th attempt waits about 8 seconds; however, attempts start at 0, so attempt 3 corresponds to 2^3=8 seconds, thus the next delay is 16 seconds.

questions.question: How does full jitter affect the delay calculation in exponential backoff?
options: Delay is a random value between zero and the base delay
Delay is doubled every retry without randomness
Delay is fixed at the base value
Delay is always the maximum allowed delay
questions.explanation: Full jitter computes delay as a random value between zero and the base exponential backoff delay to spread retries randomly.

questions.question: What is a risk of not using exponential backoff with jitter in a large-scale client reconnect scenario?
options: Server overload due to synchronized retry storms
Clients send too many ping messages
Clients reconnect too slowly
Clients never reconnect
questions.explanation: Without backoff and jitter, clients retry simultaneously causing a thundering herd that overloads the server.

questions.question: Why must the retry attempt counter be reset upon a successful connection in exponential backoff?
options: To increase the delay for the next retry
To synchronize retries across clients
To disable retries permanently
To prevent the delay from growing indefinitely after intermittent failures
questions.explanation: Resetting attempts on success prevents the delay from remaining high after temporary failures, allowing quick retries on future disconnects.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a heartbeat in WebSocket connections?
options: To close the connection after inactivity
To detect if a connection has silently died
To speed up message delivery
To send large data packets periodically
questions.explanation: Heartbeats are small messages sent periodically to detect connections that died without closing properly.

questions.question: How does the server detect dead WebSocket clients using heartbeats?
options: By sending ping messages and expecting pong responses
By closing connections after a fixed timeout
By monitoring client CPU usage
By waiting for clients to send ping messages
questions.explanation: The server sends ping messages and expects pong replies; clients that don't respond are considered dead and disconnected.

questions.question: Why does the server set `ws.isAlive = false` before sending a ping to a client?
options: To force the client to reconnect immediately
To detect if the client responds with a pong to set it alive again
To close the connection after ping
To mark the client as disconnected before pinging
questions.explanation: The server sets `isAlive` to false and expects a pong to reset it to true; if no pong arrives, the client is dead.

questions.question: How does the browser handle WebSocket ping and pong frames?
options: The browser closes the connection on ping
The browser automatically responds to pings with pongs invisibly
The browser requires explicit JavaScript code to respond to pings
The browser ignores ping frames
questions.explanation: Browsers handle ping and pong frames automatically without exposing them to JavaScript code.

questions.question: Why is an application-level heartbeat needed on the client side?
options: Because the browser API does not expose ping or pong events to JavaScript
Because the server never sends ping messages
Because TCP detects dead connections automatically
Because the browser does not send any pings automatically
questions.explanation: The browser WebSocket API does not expose ping or pong events, so the client must implement its own heartbeat to detect dead servers.

questions.question: What happens if the client does not receive a heartbeat tick message from the server within a set timeout?
options: The client assumes the connection is alive
The client sends a ping to the server
The client increases the heartbeat interval
The client closes the socket to trigger a reconnect
questions.explanation: If no heartbeat tick is received in time, the client closes the socket, triggering the reconnect logic.

questions.question: According to the lecture, how do primitives compare in shallow equality?
options: By value
By memory address
By type only
By reference
questions.explanation: Primitives compare by value in shallow equality as stated in the lecture.

questions.question: How do objects, arrays, and functions compare in shallow equality?
options: By type
By reference
By content
By value
questions.explanation: Objects, arrays, and functions compare by reference in shallow equality.

questions.question: If a parent component creates a new object literal on every render and passes it as a prop, what will React.memo do?
options: Throw an error
Skip the child re-render
Memoize the object automatically
Re-render the child component
questions.explanation: React.memo re-renders because the new object literal has a new reference failing shallow equality.

questions.question: Why does React.memo re-render a child if a new function is passed as a prop every time?
options: Because functions are always memoized
Because functions compare by value and the value changes
Because React.memo ignores functions
Because functions compare by reference and the reference changes
questions.explanation: Functions compare by reference, so a new function instance causes React.memo to re-render.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of relying on shallow equality when passing props to React.memo components?
options: Primitives are compared by reference causing bugs
New object or function references cause unnecessary re-renders
React.memo cannot memoize primitive props
React.memo does deep equality checks causing slowdowns
questions.explanation: New references for objects or functions cause React.memo to re-render despite unchanged data.

questions.question: Why might React.memo fail to optimize a child component even if props appear unchanged?
options: Because shallow equality fails when new references are passed for objects or functions
Because React.memo requires deep equality checking
Because React.memo ignores props on every render
Because React.memo only works for primitive props
questions.explanation: React.memo relies on shallow equality and fails if new references are passed as props.

questions.question: What does React.memo do by default when a component's props have not changed?
options: Throws an error
Always re-renders the component
Removes the component from the DOM
Skips the component's re-render
questions.explanation: React.memo skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal to the previous render.

questions.question: When does React.memo cause a component to re-render?
options: Only on initial mount
When props are not shallowly equal to previous props
Never re-renders after first render
When the component state changes
questions.explanation: React.memo re-renders if props differ by shallow equality from the previous render.

questions.question: If a child component wrapped in React.memo receives a new function prop on every parent render, what happens?
options: The child re-renders because the function reference changes
The child skips re-render because functions are ignored
The child memoizes the function automatically
The child throws an error
questions.explanation: New function references cause React.memo to re-render the child component.

questions.question: How can you prevent a React.memo child from re-rendering due to a changing callback prop?
options: Use useMemo instead of useCallback
Pass a new function on every render
Avoid passing callbacks as props
Wrap the callback in useCallback to keep its reference stable
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, preventing unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: According to the lecture's rule of thumb, when is it worth wrapping a child component in React.memo?
options: When the child is expensive to render — otherwise memoizing just adds overhead for no benefit
Always, because React.memo guarantees the child never re-renders
Only when every prop is a primitive, because React.memo cannot compare objects at all
Whenever the parent uses useMemo, because React.memo then deep-compares every prop
questions.explanation: The lecture's rule of thumb: memoizing is only worth it when the child is expensive to render or the reference is consumed by a memoized child; wrapping everything adds overhead for no benefit.

questions.question: Why is React.memo ineffective if the parent passes new object or function literals every render?
options: Because React.memo does deep equality checks
Because React.memo only works with primitive props
Because React.memo ignores props
Because shallow equality fails and React.memo re-renders the child
questions.explanation: New references cause shallow equality to fail, defeating React.memo optimization.

questions.question: What does useCallback do in React?
options: Forces a component to re-render
Keeps a function reference stable across renders if dependencies don't change
Creates a new function on every render
Memoizes a computed value
questions.explanation: useCallback memoizes a function reference and returns the same function unless dependencies change.

questions.question: When should you use useCallback according to the lecture?
options: When you want to recompute a value every render
When you want to create a new function every render
When passing callbacks to memoized child components
When memoizing computed values
questions.explanation: useCallback is needed to keep callbacks stable when passed to React.memo children.

questions.question: If a parent component passes a callback prop wrapped in useCallback to a React.memo child, what is the effect?
options: The child always re-renders
The callback is recomputed every render
The child sees a stable prop and can skip re-rendering
The child throws an error
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, enabling React.memo to skip re-render.

questions.question: What happens if you don't use useCallback when passing a callback to a React.memo child?
options: The child re-renders because it receives a new function reference every render
The child never re-renders
The callback is ignored
The child memoizes the callback automatically
questions.explanation: Without useCallback, a new function reference causes React.memo to re-render the child.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of overusing useCallback everywhere?
options: It adds overhead and dependency bugs for no benefit
It memoizes computed values instead of functions
It prevents all re-renders
It guarantees better performance always
questions.explanation: Overusing useCallback adds overhead and can cause bugs without improving performance.

questions.question: Why is useCallback necessary in combination with React.memo?
options: To create new functions every render
To force component re-renders
To keep function references stable so React.memo can skip re-renders
To memoize computed values
questions.explanation: useCallback keeps the function reference stable, which is required for React.memo optimizations.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of useMemo in React?
options: Memoizing a computed value and recomputing only when dependencies change
Always recomputing a value every render
Forcing a component to re-render
Memoizing a function reference
questions.explanation: useMemo memoizes computed values and only recomputes them when dependencies change.

questions.question: When is useMemo particularly valuable?
options: For memoizing callbacks passed to children
For forcing updates on every render
For expensive computed state derived from props or state that would otherwise recalculate every render
For creating new objects every render
questions.explanation: useMemo avoids recomputing expensive derived state when inputs have not changed.

questions.question: If you have a filtered and sorted list derived from a large array, how does useMemo help?
options: It memoizes the filter and sort functions
It skips recomputing the filter and sort if dependencies haven't changed
It recomputes filter and sort on every render
It prevents the component from rendering
questions.explanation: useMemo prevents redundant filter and sort computations if dependencies are unchanged.

questions.question: What happens if you do not use useMemo for expensive computations in React?
options: The computation is memoized by default
The computation is skipped automatically
The component never re-renders
The computation runs on every render even if inputs haven't changed
questions.explanation: Without useMemo, expensive computations run on every render regardless of input changes.

questions.question: What is a main pitfall of overusing useMemo everywhere without profiling?
options: It prevents all re-renders
It guarantees better performance in all cases
It memoizes function references instead of values
It adds overhead from dependency comparisons that can be slower than recomputing
questions.explanation: Overusing useMemo adds overhead that can degrade performance if not needed.

questions.question: Why might useMemo not improve performance if used excessively?
options: Because the cost of dependency comparison can outweigh recomputation savings
Because useMemo disables React.memo
Because useMemo memoizes functions instead of values
Because useMemo always recomputes values
questions.explanation: Dependency comparisons add overhead that can make useMemo slower than recomputing.

questions.question: What happens during the commit phase in React?
options: React creates new React elements without touching the DOM.
React schedules a re-render of a component when its state changes.
React calls the component function to compute the UI description.
React updates the DOM and runs layout effects after comparing the new and previous UI descriptions.
questions.explanation: The commit phase is when React compares the new description with the previous one and updates the DOM accordingly.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the commit phase?
options: It only updates the DOM if the new UI description differs from the previous one.
It runs the component function to generate React elements.
It always updates the DOM regardless of changes.
It happens before the render phase.
questions.explanation: React only commits changes to the DOM if the diff finds differences between the new and previous UI descriptions.

questions.question: If a component renders but the commit phase finds no changes, what is true?

The DOM is rebuilt from scratch.
The component's state is reset.
The component's function ran but the DOM was not updated.

questions.question: In the dashboard example, why do thousands of PriceRow components render but only a few commit?

Because React always commits all rendered components.
Because the commit phase happens before the render phase.
Because many render computations are done but only rows with changed data cause DOM updates.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall related to the commit phase in React performance?
options: Using deep equality checks instead of shallow equality.
Believing that React never re-renders children when a parent renders.
Assuming that renders always update the DOM, leading to unnecessary optimization efforts.
Updating state inside the commit phase.
questions.explanation: Many think renders always cause DOM updates, but commit only updates if the UI description changed, so optimizing all renders is unnecessary.

questions.question: Why is it important to distinguish between render and commit phases when optimizing React apps?
options: Because commit phase runs before render phase.
Because only the commit phase can cause re-renders.
Because renders can be cheap and harmless, but unnecessary commits cause expensive DOM updates.
Because render phase updates the DOM directly.
questions.explanation: Understanding that renders don't always update the DOM helps focus optimization on avoiding unnecessary commits, which are costly.

questions.question: Which of the following triggers a React component to re-render?

Reassigning a variable inside the component.
Calling a setter with the same value.
Changing a ref value.
questions.explanation: State updates schedule a re-render, while changing refs or variables inside a component do not trigger re-renders.

questions.question: What causes all children of a component to re-render by default?
options: When the child's props change.
When the parent component re-renders.
When the child's state changes.
When a ref changes.
questions.explanation: React renders all children recursively when a parent renders, regardless of whether props changed.

questions.question: If a parent component re-renders but the child's props remain the same, what happens to the child?
options: The child never re-renders unless its props change.
The child skips rendering automatically.
The child unmounts and remounts.
The child still re-renders because its parent rendered.
questions.explanation: By default, children re-render whenever their parent renders, even if their props have not changed.

questions.question: Why does the dashboard re-render all 5,000 PriceRow components on every tick even though only a few prices change?
options: Because the state that holds prices is high in the tree, causing all descendants to re-render.
Because the filter state changed.
Because refs changed in each PriceRow.
Because React automatically re-renders only changed rows.
questions.explanation: State updates high in the tree cause the entire subtree to re-render, including all PriceRow components.

questions.question: What is a common misconception about what triggers a child component to re-render?
options: That changing a ref triggers re-renders.
That a child re-renders because its props changed, whereas it actually re-renders because its parent rendered.
That context changes do not trigger re-renders.
That state changes never trigger re-renders.
questions.explanation: The lecture clarifies that children re-render because their parent rendered, not because their props changed.

questions.question: Why might calling a setter with the same value still cause a component to render once more?
options: Because context changed.
Because React always re-renders on any setter call.
Because React may render once before bailing out even if the value is unchanged.
Because refs changed instead of state.
questions.explanation: React usually bails out on same value setters but may still render once before skipping further renders.

questions.question: What does reference stability mean in React?
options: Keeping the same object, array, or function reference when the data hasn't changed.
Creating new objects on every render for safety.
Avoiding useMemo and useCallback hooks.
Using deep equality checks to compare props.
questions.explanation: Reference stability means preserving the same references so shallow equality checks succeed and avoid unnecessary renders.

questions.question: Why do two objects with identical contents but different references cause re-renders?
options: Because primitives are compared by reference.
Because React ignores object props.
Because React deeply compares all props.
Because React uses shallow equality which compares references, not deep contents.

questions.question: If a parent creates a new array inline every render and passes it as a prop, what happens to a memoized child component receiving that prop?
options: It skips re-render because React does deep equality on arrays.
It re-renders every time because the array reference changes.
It throws an error.

questions.question: Why should functions be memoized with useCallback in React?
options: Because useCallback deeply compares function bodies.
Because functions never change references.
Because functions are objects and new function references cause re-renders if passed as props.
Because React ignores functions as props.
questions.explanation: New function references cause shallow equality to fail, so useCallback keeps the same function reference to avoid re-renders.

questions.question: What is a pitfall of shallow equality checks in React memoization?
options: They cause React to skip all renders.
They do not detect changes inside nested objects, causing unnecessary re-renders if references change even without meaningful data changes.
They perform expensive deep comparisons.
They ignore primitive props.

questions.question: Why does React use shallow equality instead of deep equality for prop comparisons?
options: Because deep equality is not possible in JavaScript.
Because React does not care about prop changes.
Because deep comparisons would be expensive and slow down rendering.
Because shallow equality is more accurate.
questions.explanation: Deep comparison of large data structures would be costly, so React uses cheap shallow equality checks.

questions.question: What does the render phase in React do?
options: Calls the component function to compute a UI description without touching the DOM.
Compares new and old UI descriptions.
Schedules state updates.
Updates the DOM and runs layout effects.

questions.question: During the render phase, what is created?
options: State updates.
DOM nodes and text nodes.
A tree of React elements describing the UI.
Layout effects.

questions.question: If a component's render function returns the same description as last time, what happens during commit?

The DOM is rebuilt completely.
The component is unmounted.
No DOM updates occur because the diff finds no differences.

options: Because renders skip the commit phase.
Because React always updates the DOM on every render.
Because renders cause state resets.
Because the component function runs but the UI description does not change, so no DOM update is needed.

options: It deeply compares all props to skip renders.
It avoids all unnecessary renders by default.
It favors correctness and simplicity over performance, assuming renders are cheap but causing many unnecessary renders.
It only renders children when their props change.
questions.explanation: React's default behavior is to render all children on parent render for correctness, even if it causes many unnecessary renders.

questions.question: Why should developers focus on avoiding renders that don't change anything rather than avoiding all renders?
options: Because avoiding all renders breaks React.
Because renders are usually cheap, but unnecessary renders that produce no UI changes cause wasted JavaScript work.
Because React does not allow skipping renders.
Because commit phase is expensive and must be avoided.

The component caused a wasted render
The component rendered with updated props

questions.question: What does a wide rectangle in the flame graph represent?

These components are rendering correctly due to prop changes

The frequency of user interactions

options: Memoize the child components to avoid unnecessary renders
Remove the ranked view to simplify analysis
Disable the flame graph
Increase the state in the parent component

questions.question: What does a single fat bar in the ranked view suggest about render cost?
options: An expensive computation in one component rather than many cheap renders
The component is not rendering at all
The component has many children rendering cheaply
The render cost is evenly distributed
questions.explanation: The transcript explains a fat single bar means one expensive computation rather than many cheap renders.

questions.question: What is a trade-off when state is lifted too high in the component tree?
options: It prevents the flame graph from showing wasted renders
It reduces the number of commits recorded

Everything beneath re-renders on every state change, increasing render cost

Because they are ignored by React DevTools Profiler
Because they create new references on every render, causing re-renders

questions.question: What clue does the Profiler give to identify wasted renders?
options: The component appears as gray in the flame graph

Immediately optimize it with memoization
Ignore it since the cost is negligible

Because the ranked view hides them

questions.question: What is a pitfall of having too much state in a high-level component like Dashboard?
options: It reduces the render cost of PriceRow components
It automatically memoizes all child components
It causes all child components to re-render on every state change, leading to wasted renders
It prevents the commit chart from displaying correctly

questions.question: What is the risk of recomputing filtering and sorting on every render?
options: It increases render cost unnecessarily, even if the sort order hasn't changed
It causes components to appear gray in the flame graph
It reduces the number of commits recorded

questions.explanation: The transcript warns that recomputing filtering and sorting on every render causes unnecessary render cost.
