questions.question: Why is memoization particularly useful for computed state derived from props or other state?
options: Because it delays rendering until user interaction
Because it forces React to re-render more often
Because it caches expensive computations and skips them when inputs are unchanged
Because it automatically updates dependencies
questions.explanation: Memoization caches expensive computed state results and skips recomputation when inputs remain the same.

questions.question: What is computed state in the context of React performance optimization?
options: State that is stored in a parent component and passed down as props
State that triggers re-renders of all child components
State that is derived from props or other state values and recalculated on every render
State that is memoized using useCallback
questions.explanation: Computed state is derived from props or other state values and would otherwise be recalculated on every render even when inputs have not changed, as explained in Lecture 3.2.

questions.question: Given a large list filtered by a search string and sorted by a key, when should you recompute the filtered and sorted list?
options: Only when the user clicks a button
Only when the component mounts
On every render regardless of inputs
Only when the list, filter string, or sort key change
questions.explanation: Memoization allows recomputing only when dependencies like list, filter, or sort key change.

questions.question: If you have a component that filters and sorts a large list based on user input, when should you recompute the filtered and sorted list?
options: On every render regardless of input changes
Only when the list, filter string, or sort key change
Only when the component mounts
Only when the user clicks a button
questions.explanation: The filtered and sorted list should be recomputed only when its inputs (rows array, filter string, or sort key) change, as memoization depends on these dependencies.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of memoizing a computed value whose dependencies change on nearly every render?
options: It causes unnecessary overhead because the cache never hits
It automatically optimizes performance
It causes stale data to be displayed
It prevents the component from re-rendering
questions.explanation: Memoizing a value whose dependencies change every render adds overhead without savings because the cache never hits, as explained in Lecture 3.3.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: Why is forgetting a dependency in a useMemo dependency array dangerous?
options: Because it increases the memory usage of the component
Because React will not recompute the memoized value when that dependency changes, causing stale or wrong output
Because it triggers unnecessary child component re-renders
Because it causes React to recompute the value on every render
questions.explanation: Forgetting a dependency causes React to skip recomputation when that dependency changes, resulting in stale or incorrect output, as highlighted in Lecture 3.3.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: What is the main benefit of lifting content up when a stateful wrapper surrounds slow content?
options: It disables React's reconciliation
It forces re-creation of children on every render
It duplicates the children elements
It stabilizes children element references to prevent unnecessary re-renders
questions.explanation: Lifting content up allows the parent to create children elements, keeping their references stable and preventing re-renders.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What does the technique 'lifting content up' involve in React optimization?
options: Passing expensive children as a children prop from a parent component to avoid re-creating them on wrapper state changes
Moving state down into smaller components that use it
Using useMemo to memoize computed values
Wrapping components with React.memo to prevent re-renders
questions.explanation: Lifting content up means rendering the expensive children in a parent and passing them as children props to avoid re-creation on wrapper state changes, as explained in Lecture 3.1.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: If a component holds state and wraps expensive children, what technique can prevent unnecessary re-renders of those children?
options: Wrapping children in useMemo
Passing the children as a prop from the parent component
Duplicating state in each child
Moving state down into the children
questions.explanation: Passing children as a prop from the parent creates stable references, so the wrapper's state changes don't cause children to re-render.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: Why does passing children as a prop help avoid re-renders when a wrapper component's state changes?
options: Because children passed as props are memoized automatically
Because React always re-renders children passed as props
Because children passed as props are ignored during re-render
Because the children prop reference stays the same if created in the parent
questions.explanation: When children are created in the parent, their reference remains stable, so React skips re-rendering them when the wrapper's state changes.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What is the trade-off when lifting content up to avoid re-renders?
options: It requires duplicating state in multiple places
It may complicate component structure but stabilizes child references
It disables memoization hooks
It increases the number of components rendered
questions.explanation: Lifting content up can complicate the component hierarchy but stabilizes references, preventing unnecessary re-renders.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What is a trade-off when lifting content up to avoid re-renders of expensive children?
options: It prevents the use of React.memo on children
It requires adding useMemo everywhere
The parent component must create the children element, which may increase coupling
State must be duplicated in multiple components
questions.explanation: Lifting content up requires the parent to create the children element, which can increase coupling but avoids re-renders when the wrapper's state changes, as described in Lecture 3.1.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What does memoization do in React?
options: Delays rendering until user interaction
Caches the result of a computation to avoid recomputing with unchanged inputs
Duplicates state to improve performance
Automatically updates state on prop change
questions.explanation: Memoization caches computation results and returns the cached result if inputs have not changed.

questions.question: Which React hook is used to memoize computed values?
options: useEffect
useMemo
useCallback
useState
questions.explanation: useMemo memoizes computed values and recomputes them only when dependencies change.

questions.question: How does useMemo determine whether to recompute a value?
options: By comparing dependencies with deep equality
By always recomputing on every render
By comparing dependencies with Object.is shallow equality
By checking if the component's state changed
questions.explanation: useMemo uses Object.is shallow equality to compare dependencies and decide if recomputation is needed.

questions.question: How does React.memo combined with useCallback help prevent unnecessary child renders?
options: React.memo and useCallback are unrelated
React.memo disables re-renders and useCallback delays rendering
React.memo memoizes functions and useCallback memoizes values
React.memo memoizes components and useCallback memoizes callback function references
questions.explanation: React.memo memoizes components to avoid re-renders, and useCallback memoizes callbacks to keep stable function references.

questions.question: What is the recommended first step before using memoization to optimize performance?
options: Use React.memo on all components
Ignore performance issues
Move state down or restructure components
Add useMemo everywhere
questions.explanation: The recommended first step is to move state down or restructure components to reduce unnecessary renders before memoizing.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: What is a key pitfall when memoizing computed state in React?
options: Not using React.memo on child components
Moving state down instead of up
Memoizing functions instead of values
Using incorrect or incomplete dependency arrays causing stale or wrong output
questions.explanation: A key pitfall is forgetting dependencies in the useMemo array, which causes stale or incorrect output, as explained in Lecture 3.3.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: Where should state be placed to minimize unnecessary re-renders?
options: In a global store
In a sibling component
In the highest common ancestor component
In the component that directly uses the state
questions.explanation: Moving state down into the component that needs it reduces the subtree that re-renders when the state changes.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What is the effect of moving the hoveredSymbol state from Dashboard to SymbolTooltip?
options: All rows re-render on hover
Dashboard and all its children re-render on hover
Only SymbolTooltip re-renders on hover
No components re-render on hover
questions.explanation: Moving hoveredSymbol state down to SymbolTooltip limits re-renders to only that small component on hover.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What happens when you move filter state down into FilterBar if the filter is needed by both FilterBar and the table?
options: You cannot move the filter state down because it is shared
The filter state updates automatically everywhere
The table cannot access the filter state anymore
The filter state is duplicated and inconsistent
questions.explanation: If state is genuinely needed by multiple components, it cannot be moved down into just one of them.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: If a piece of state is only used by a small tooltip component, what is the benefit of moving that state down into the tooltip component?
options: The entire dashboard re-renders more efficiently
Only the tooltip re-renders on state change, avoiding re-rendering large subtrees
It enables memoization of the tooltip state
It prevents the tooltip from updating
questions.explanation: Moving state down limits re-renders to the small subtree that uses it, improving performance, as demonstrated with hoveredSymbol in Lecture 3.1.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What is a key pitfall when moving state down to optimize rendering?
options: State might be duplicated in multiple components
State can no longer be memoized
State might become inaccessible to components that need it
State updates become asynchronous
questions.explanation: Moving state down can be problematic if multiple components need the same state, making it inaccessible if placed too low.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: Why might moving state down be preferred over adding useMemo for performance optimization?
options: Because useMemo caches only functions
Because useMemo does not work for state
Because moving state down reduces the subtree re-rendered without overhead
Because moving state down always disables re-rendering
questions.explanation: Moving state down reduces the number of components re-rendered without the overhead of memoization dependency checks.
questions.lecture: 3.1 - Moving State Down and Lifting Content Up

questions.question: What is the overhead cost associated with each useMemo call?
options: Increasing the size of the component's state
Creating new function references on every render
Storing the previous value, dependency array, and comparing dependencies on every render
Re-rendering all child components unnecessarily
questions.explanation: Each useMemo call stores previous value and dependencies and compares dependencies on every render, which adds overhead, as explained in Lecture 3.3.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: Why is it important to measure performance before adding useMemo to a computation?
options: Because memoizing trivial or frequently changing computations can add overhead and slow down the app
Because useMemo always improves performance regardless of cost
Because useMemo automatically fixes stale dependency bugs
Because useMemo replaces the need to move state down
questions.explanation: Measuring helps avoid memoizing trivial or frequently changing computations that add overhead and degrade performance, as advised in Lecture 3.3.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: What is a key rule of thumb before applying useMemo for performance?
options: Use useMemo only for state variables
Apply useMemo to all computations regardless of cost
Measure if the computation is slow and inputs often stay the same
Avoid useMemo completely
questions.explanation: Use useMemo only if the computation is measurably slow and its inputs often remain unchanged.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: Why is it important to have the ESLint rule react-hooks/exhaustive-deps enabled when using useMemo?
options: To catch missing dependencies that cause stale memoized values
To automatically memoize all dependencies
To disable memoization when dependencies change
To optimize dependency comparison speed
questions.explanation: The rule catches missing dependencies in the array, preventing stale or incorrect memoized outputs.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: What is a potential downside of overusing useMemo everywhere without profiling?
options: It always improves performance
It causes state to become stale
It adds overhead from dependency comparisons that can slow down rendering
It disables React's reconciliation
questions.explanation: Overusing useMemo adds overhead from dependency checks that can outweigh the benefits if computations are cheap.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: Why can memoizing a value whose dependencies change every render be counterproductive?
options: Because the cached value is always reused
Because React skips the computation
Because it causes infinite loops
Because memoization overhead is paid but cache never hits
questions.explanation: If dependencies change every render, the cache never hits and the overhead of memoization is wasted.
questions.lecture: 3.3 - When useMemo Costs More Than It Saves

questions.question: What does React.memo do when wrapping a component?
options: Only works with primitive props, ignoring objects and functions
Prevents any re-rendering regardless of prop changes
Skips re-rendering if props are shallowly equal to previous props
Always re-renders the component on every parent render
questions.explanation: React.memo wraps a component and skips the re-render when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render.

questions.question: Why did wrapping PriceRow with React.memo alone not reduce re-renders?
options: Because the parent component never re-rendered
Because all props were primitive values
Because React.memo does not work with function components
Because the onSelect prop was a new function reference each render
questions.explanation: The onSelect callback was recreated inline on every render, causing a new function reference and defeating React.memo's shallow prop comparison.

questions.question: If a parent component passes a new inline function as a prop to many memoized children, what happens?
options: Children re-render only if their internal state changes
Children skip re-rendering because React.memo ignores functions
Only children with changed primitive props re-render
All children re-render because shallow equality fails on the function prop
questions.explanation: New inline functions create new references each render, causing React.memo to see changed props and re-render all children.

questions.question: How does wrapping a callback with useCallback help when used with React.memo children?
options: It keeps the function reference stable, allowing children to skip re-renders
It forces the function to be recreated every render for safety
It memoizes the child's internal state
It prevents the parent component from re-rendering
questions.explanation: useCallback returns the same function instance as long as dependencies don't change, stabilizing the prop reference for memoized children.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of using React.memo with inline objects or functions as props?
options: Inline objects are deeply compared, causing performance issues
Memoization silently fails because new references cause re-renders without warning
React.memo throws an error if inline objects are passed
Inline functions are automatically memoized by React.memo
questions.explanation: Inline objects and functions create new references each render, causing React.memo to re-render without any warning or error.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: Why is React.memo ineffective against re-render storms caused by context updates?
options: Because React.memo disables context updates
Because React.memo only works with class components
Because context updates cause all consumers to re-render regardless of memoization
Because context values are always primitive
questions.explanation: When a context value changes, every component using useContext re-renders regardless of React.memo, which only guards against parent-driven re-renders.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: What is a common cause of React.memo being defeated by inline objects in props?
options: React.memo cannot wrap function components
Passing only primitive props causes memo to fail
Inline objects are deeply compared causing slow renders
Passing object literals directly in JSX creates new references every render
questions.explanation: Inline object literals like style={{color: 'green'}} create new references each render, causing shallow equality to fail and memo to re-render.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: Why does passing an inline function like onRemove={() => removeSymbol(r.symbol)} break memo optimization?
options: Because a new function is created on every render, changing the prop reference
Because arrow functions are not supported by React.memo
Because removeSymbol is not memoized
Because the child component ignores function props
questions.explanation: Each inline arrow function creates a new function object every render, causing React.memo to detect a changed prop and re-render.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: Given a component that needs to pass a function with an argument to a memoized child, what is a good pattern to avoid breaking memo?
options: Pass a stable callback function and the argument separately, letting the child call the function with the argument
Pass the function as children instead of a prop
Always create a new inline function with the argument on each render
Avoid passing functions as props altogether
questions.explanation: Passing a stable function and the argument separately lets the child call the function internally, avoiding new function references per render.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: What debugging approach helps identify which prop is causing a memoized component to re-render?
options: Wrap the component with useMemo instead
Disable React.memo temporarily
Record in the Profiler with why-rendered setting and check the tooltip for blamed props
Use console.log inside the child component's render
questions.explanation: The Profiler with why-rendered enabled shows which prop changed and caused the re-render, helping find inline objects or functions.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: Why does passing JSX as children to a memoized component cause re-renders?
options: Because memoized components cannot accept children
Because JSX creates a new element object each render, changing the children prop reference
Because JSX elements are deeply compared and always differ
Because children props are ignored by React.memo
questions.explanation: JSX creates a new React element object every render, so the children prop reference changes, defeating React.memo's shallow comparison.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: What trade-off is involved in hoisting constant objects outside a component to fix memo issues?
options: You create a stable reference but lose the ability to compute the object based on props or state
You must rewrite the component as a class
You disable React.memo for that component
You increase memory usage drastically
questions.explanation: Hoisting constants creates stable references but means the object cannot depend on dynamic props or state values.
questions.lecture: 4.2 - Inline Objects and Functions That Break memo

questions.question: What happens to components consuming a context when the context value changes?
options: React.memo prevents re-renders on context changes
Only components with changed props re-render
Only components that use useState re-render
All consuming components re-render regardless of React.memo
questions.explanation: When a context value changes, all components using useContext for that context re-render, ignoring React.memo.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: Why does creating the context provider value as an object literal inside the provider cause excessive re-renders?
options: Because React requires context values to be primitives
Because a new object reference is created every render, causing all consumers to see a changed value
Because context providers only accept functions as values
Because object literals are deeply compared causing slow renders
questions.explanation: An object literal inside the provider is recreated each render, so consumers see a new reference and re-render even if fields didn't change.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: How does splitting context into multiple smaller contexts reduce re-render storms?
options: It merges all state into one big context to optimize updates
It forces all consumers to re-render simultaneously
Components only subscribe to contexts with values they need, so unrelated changes don't cause re-renders
It disables context updates for memoized components
questions.explanation: Splitting context lets components subscribe only to relevant pieces, so changes in unrelated context parts don't trigger their re-renders.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: Why is memoizing context provider values with useMemo important?
options: It prevents any context consumers from updating
It forces the provider to re-render every time
It ensures the context value reference only changes when its actual contents change
It converts context values into primitives automatically
questions.explanation: useMemo stabilizes the provider value reference so consumers only re-render on actual changes, avoiding unnecessary re-renders.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: What is a subtle pitfall of context that causes re-render storms despite memoization?
options: Context only works with class components
Context has no selector, so any change to any part of the value re-renders all consumers
React.memo disables context updates automatically
Context values are deeply compared causing slow renders
questions.explanation: Context consumers re-render on any change to the entire value object because context does not support partial subscriptions or selectors.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: What is the benefit of separating state values and their setters into different contexts?
options: Components that only trigger updates with setters do not re-render on state changes
It merges multiple contexts into one
It forces all components to re-render on every update
It disables React.memo for those components
questions.explanation: Setters are stable references, so putting them in their own context prevents components that only use setters from re-rendering when state changes.
questions.lecture: 4.3 - Splitting Context to Stop Re-render Storms

questions.question: What does useDeferredValue do when you receive a prop value that changes frequently?
options: It batches multiple updates into a single render
It immediately updates the value and blocks rendering until done
It cancels the update if a new one arrives before rendering finishes
It defers the update and first renders with the old value, then re-renders in the background with the new value
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue first renders with the old deferred value, then re-renders in the background with the new one, making urgent updates finish fast.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: When should you prefer useDeferredValue over useTransition according to the lecture?
options: When you want to block input updates
When you want to control the state setter directly
When the update is urgent and must be immediate
When you only receive a value via props and don't control the setter
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue is used when you only receive a value and don't control the setter, while useTransition is for when you control the setter.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: If you have an input controlled by a prop value that updates frequently and causes lag, how would useDeferredValue help?
options: It would batch all prop updates and apply them at once
It would prevent the input from updating until rendering completes
It would delay the expensive rendering triggered by the prop, keeping the input responsive
It would cancel any previous renders and only render the latest prop value
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue delays the expensive rendering triggered by the prop value, so urgent updates finish fast and the input stays responsive.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: How can useDeferredValue be applied in a scenario where you cannot split input state and filter state?
options: By wrapping the input's onChange handler in startTransition
By throttling the input updates manually
By memoizing the input component to avoid re-renders
By deferring the filter value used for rendering the table rows, so the input updates immediately
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue defers the filter value used for rendering, allowing the input to update immediately even if you can't split states.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: Why doesn't useDeferredValue make the total rendering work faster?
options: Because it caches all rendered components
Because it only prioritizes updates, sometimes causing interrupted renders to restart
Because it blocks urgent updates until deferred updates complete
Because it batches all updates into a single render cycle
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue prioritizes urgent updates but can cause interrupted renders to restart, so total work is the same or slightly more.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: What is a key limitation of updates inside a transition mentioned in the lecture?
options: They can't be used to control a text input directly
They cause all renders to be synchronous
They always block urgent updates
They only work with timers and fetches
questions.explanation: Updates inside a transition can't be used to control a text input directly, which is why inputValue was kept separate.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: What does useTransition provide besides marking an update as low priority?
options: Automatic memoization of components
A method to batch multiple state updates
An isPending boolean to indicate if the transition is in progress
A way to defer prop updates
questions.explanation: useTransition returns isPending, which is true while the transition update is in progress, allowing UI feedback like dimming.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: How does useTransition keep the input responsive during expensive table updates?
options: By batching the input and table updates together
By skipping the table update until the input stops changing
By rendering the input update immediately and the table update in the background as a low-priority transition
By memoizing the input component
questions.explanation: useTransition renders the input update immediately and the table update as a low-priority background transition, keeping input responsive.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: In a scenario where the user types quickly, what does React do with in-progress transition renders?
options: It ignores new updates until the current render finishes
It merges all renders into one
It interrupts and discards the in-progress render to process the urgent update first
It queues all renders and processes them sequentially
questions.explanation: React interrupts and discards in-progress transition renders if a more urgent update arrives, prioritizing urgent updates.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: How can you visually indicate that a transition update is pending in the UI?
options: By hiding the component until the update finishes
By showing a loading spinner inside the input
By dimming the component using opacity based on isPending
By disabling the input field
questions.explanation: You can dim the component using opacity controlled by isPending to show that the transition update is catching up.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: Why should transitions be used only after applying real optimizations?
options: Because transitions block all other updates
Because transitions don't reduce total work and may add overhead by interrupting renders
Because transitions make the app slower by design
Because transitions only work on timers and fetches
questions.explanation: Transitions don't reduce total work and can add overhead, so real optimizations should be done first before using transitions.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: What is a trade-off when using useTransition for UI updates?
options: The total render work may increase due to interrupted and restarted renders
The input becomes unresponsive during transitions
Transitions block all other state updates
Transitions disable memoization
questions.explanation: Transitions may increase total render work because interrupted renders are discarded and restarted, trading off throughput for responsiveness.
questions.lecture: 5.2 - useTransition and useDeferredValue for Lag-Free Filtering

questions.question: What is virtualization (or windowing) in the context of rendering large tables?
options: Rendering rows only when the user clicks on them
Rendering only the visible rows plus a small buffer, faking the rest
Rendering rows one at a time in sequence
Rendering all rows but memoizing each row
questions.explanation: Virtualization renders only the visible rows plus a buffer, and fakes the rest to improve performance with large lists.

questions.question: What problem does virtualization solve when rendering thousands of rows?
options: It batches all row renders into one update
It reduces the number of DOM nodes mounted, improving initial load and scroll performance
It memoizes each row to avoid re-renders
It disables rendering of rows outside the viewport permanently
questions.explanation: Virtualization reduces the number of DOM nodes mounted by rendering only visible rows, improving load and scroll performance.

questions.question: If a table container has height 600px and each row is 32px tall, how many rows should virtualization render to fill the viewport?
options: All 5000 rows
Only 1 row
Exactly 600 rows
About 19 rows plus an overscan buffer
questions.explanation: 600 / 32 = 18.75, so about 19 visible rows plus an overscan buffer are rendered in virtualization.

questions.question: How does virtualization handle the scrollbar to make it behave as if all rows exist?
options: By disabling scrolling
By rendering all rows offscreen
By rendering a tall empty div with total height equal to all rows' combined height
By hiding the scrollbar entirely
questions.explanation: Virtualization renders a tall empty div with the full scroll height so the scrollbar behaves as if all rows exist.

questions.question: Why is virtualization not free despite its performance benefits?
options: Because it disables memoization
Because browser find-in-page and screen readers can't access rows not in the DOM
Because it increases the number of DOM nodes
Because it requires all rows to be rendered at least once
questions.explanation: Virtualization hides rows from the DOM, so find-in-page and screen readers lose some context, requiring extra accessibility attributes.

questions.question: What is a key implementation detail to keep memoization effective when using virtualization?
options: Avoid using React.memo on rows
Render all rows but hide them with CSS
Compute the row offset inside the row component from an index prop instead of inline style objects
Use inline style objects with new references each render
questions.explanation: Computing offset inside the row from an index prop avoids creating new inline style objects each render, preserving memoization.

questions.question: What is windowing in the context of rendering large lists?
options: Rendering items in fixed-size pages
Rendering all items but hiding them with CSS
Rendering items only when the user scrolls to them
Another term for virtualization, rendering only visible items plus a buffer
questions.explanation: Windowing is another name for virtualization, rendering only visible items plus a small buffer.

questions.question: Why do we add an overscan buffer in windowing/virtualization?
options: To disable scrolling temporarily
To reduce the total number of rows rendered to zero
To render a few extra rows above and below the viewport to avoid blank gaps during fast scrolling
To render all rows at once
questions.explanation: Overscan renders extra rows around the visible window to prevent blank gaps when scrolling quickly.

questions.question: How does windowing calculate which rows to render when the user scrolls?
options: By rendering rows randomly
By rendering only the first 20 rows always
By rendering all rows and hiding the invisible ones
By using scrollTop divided by row height to find the first visible index, then slicing rows accordingly
questions.explanation: Windowing calculates the first visible row as Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT) and slices rows to render only those visible plus overscan.

questions.question: What style positioning is used for rows in windowing to place them correctly in the scroll container?
options: Static positioning with no offset
Absolute positioning with top offset based on row index and row height
Fixed positioning at the top of the container
Relative positioning with margin
questions.explanation: Rows are absolutely positioned with top set to index * ROW_HEIGHT to place them correctly in the scroll container.

questions.question: What accessibility trade-off does windowing introduce?
options: It prevents find-in-page from working on visible rows
It disables keyboard navigation entirely
Screen readers lose context because rows not in the DOM are invisible
It makes the scrollbar inaccessible
questions.explanation: Rows not in the DOM are invisible to screen readers, so windowing requires adding aria attributes to maintain context.

questions.question: Why is virtualization/windowing done after cheap fixes like memoization?
options: Because virtualization is always slower than memoization
Because virtualization requires all rows to be rendered first
Because memoization disables virtualization
Because virtualization is more complex and has trade-offs, so simpler optimizations should be applied first
questions.explanation: Virtualization has trade-offs and complexity, so it's applied after cheaper fixes like memoization improve performance.

questions.question: What is a key reason components re-render in React according to the lecture?
options: Because their parent rendered
Because their props changed
Because the DOM changed
Because the component was mounted
questions.explanation: Components re-render because of state, context, or because their parent rendered, never simply because props changed.

questions.question: Which React hook is used to cache expensive derived values to optimize rendering?
options: useEffect
useCallback
useState
useMemo
questions.explanation: useMemo caches expensive derived values to avoid unnecessary recalculations.

questions.question: If a component's inline style object changes every render, what is the likely impact on memo boundaries?
options: Memo boundaries will work as expected
Memo boundaries will cause the component to unmount
Memo boundaries will break because the style object reference changes
Memo boundaries will improve performance
questions.explanation: Inline objects like style objects break memo boundaries because their references change every render, causing unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: In a scenario where a component receives stable props but its parent re-renders frequently, what can help prevent unnecessary re-renders?
options: Removing useCallback hooks
Adding more inline functions
Increasing the component's state
Using React.memo on the component
questions.explanation: React.memo helps prevent unnecessary re-renders by memoizing the component and skipping renders when props are stable.

questions.question: What is a maintenance cost associated with adding memo boundaries and dependency arrays?
options: They increase bundle size significantly
They require rewriting components in class syntax
They add complexity requiring comments to explain their purpose
They reduce code readability

questions.question: Why is it important to remove optimizations that do not improve performance after profiling?

Because they increase the number of commits
Because they clutter the codebase and make future changes harder
Because they always cause bugs

It forces you to write more inline functions
